["Both. Our provincial government finds it necessary, because of this large influx of ignorant and uneducated people, to bring in a compulsory educational Bill at this session of the legislature and it is not right that they should be compelled to incur a largely increased expenditure for this purpose, that they can ill afford, on account of the policy of the Minister of the Interior. And I hope in this connection that this government 'will hand over to the province of Manitoba the school lands and the school funds now held in trust for that province and properly belonging to it, to be administered by the local authorities for educational purposes, as they are in a much better position to do so to better advantage than the Dominion government can possibly hope to be.
It has been claimed by our opponents that the days of the exodus are past, and our people no longer seek homes in the country to the south of us. But, I find on looking at the Trade and Navigation Returns that settlers effects to the amount of $1.0yj,53ii, were exported from our country during the last year, which is a pretty good index that the exodus against which they declaimed so loudly in years gone by, is still in existence.
Railway subsidies and steamship subventions which came in for so much denunciation at the hands of hon. gentlemen opposite when they were on this side of the House, I notice are still being voted as in the days of the Conservative administration only more so. Millions of dollars of public funds are annually voted for railways without any adequate return to the people, which has possibly done more to create that agitation for government ownership, an agitation that first arose in the progressive province of Manitoba, and which is gaining force every day in other portions of the Dominion, than almost any other act of the government.
In the matter of steamship subventions, our farmers were told that the country was bonusing vessels to ply between Australia and Vancouver to bring into unfair competition with our mutton the mutton from the Australian colony. They did not tell the farmers that before a pound of that mutton could be landed on Canadian territory it had to pay a duty of 35 per cent under Conservative administration. Actually Liberal campaginers hawked auout cans of Australian mutton as an illustration of the unfair competition our farmers were being subjected to. After carrying on such a warfare you would imagine these gentlemen, on coming into power, would have taken the first opportunity either to abolish the steamship subventions or at least to raise the duties, and thus give more protection to our farmers.
Did they do so ? Why, on the contrary we see that steamship subventions are continued as much as they ever were in the past ; and not only that, but, mutton is being imported in increased quantities under the tariff which gives a preference of 33J per cent. In looking up the Trade and Navigation Returns, I found that in 1S9G we imported into Canada 22,299 pounds of mutton, the duty being then 35 per cent. Last year, ending 30th June, 1900, we imported the enormous quantity of 565,401 pounds, which paid a duty reduced by 331 per cent. So, if our farmers were suffering and burdened by this keen competition in 1896, how much keener must that competition be when thirty times as much mutton is being imported under the reduction of 331 per cent. When the tariff was submitted to the House in 1897 by the present government, it created a great deal of dissatisfaction amongst the western people, and even among the western representatives, because they knew the pledges upon which they had secured their seats. They knew that promises were held out to the people that they should get their raw material free. When the tariff was brought down the Liberal speakers had to do what they could to let themselves down easy. They told us that, of course, we could not expect the government, at one feel swoop- to use a favourite expression of the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright)-to give us free trade. We were to have free trade on the instalment plan. But year after year lias gone by, and now instalments are overdue. No further instalments have been paid, and free trade- on the instalment plan has not been effected, and is not the shibboleth of the Liberal party to-day. Free agricultural implements was the cry of the past. We heard denunciations of the rebates on duties paid to the manufacturers of implements to enable them to send machines to farmers living in foreign countries thousands of miles away, to enable them to buy those implements cheaply, and to compete with our own farmers at an advantage. I find by the return brought down in response to a motion presented by myself that these drawbacks are still continued, and that, for the year ending 30th June last, they amounted to 8245,151.46. Now, I might go on and comment upon the extravagance of the government, but that point has been so fully covered that I need not occupy the time of the House. We all know that the public debt, which, we were promised would be reduced, has been increased by $7,000,000 : that the expenditures which were to have been reduced by one, two, or three millions, have gone up by fourteen millions; that the taxation of the country, which was to have been cut down has also been increased by", 'several millions-and still tlie carnival of extravagance goes merrily on. It is time tliat this government should call a halt to the useless waste of public money. If they are not able, during a time of great prosperity, when we have great expansion in our imports and our exports, when the trade of the country has been leaping up as it has been-if they are not able, notwithstanding that millions of dollars have been wrung out of the pockets of the people as a surplus by unnecessary and unjust taxation, to reduce our expenditure or to apply any portion of the surplus to reduce the national debt, how can we expect to effect such a reduction when we are sliding down the wave, upon the crest of which we now are, according to the Finance Minister. In the time of prosperity wise statesmen prepare for adversity. Otherwise the reaction that is sure to set in will create a commercial panic, and already there seems some sign of an approaching period of depression. While we are not pessimists-and, in that respect we differ from hou. gentlemen on the other side, for we do not believe in decrying the fair fame of our country for the sake of gaining a petty political advantage-yet, as citizens of the country, when we see the government drifting recklessly along, it is our duty to warn them of the approaching storm so that by cutting down their expenditure, and by judicious admiuistratiou, they may fortify the country against commercial disaster. In accordance with my usual custom, I will not trespass long upon the patience of the House, but will content myself with these remarks, seeing that the subject has been so thoroughly threshed out.

Mr. Speaker, for the statement which I am about to make, I have probably tbe same kind of authority as my hon. friend (Mr. Wallace), who last addressed the House, had for a number of statements which he made in the course of his speech. My statement is that I have received confidential communications in regard to a conference that took place between the hon. leader of the opposition and the advisory board that assists him in conducting the affairs of this House-

Oh, how clever.
Mr. RUSSELL-and that it was arranged among them that my hon. friend who addressed the House last night should visit North Bruce in the capacity of a peacemaker, for the purpose of setting at rest all racial, religious and discordant cries and all disturbing controversies which would otherwise have agitated that community. It was represented to him that the subject of the preferential tariff would come up for more or less discussion in the course of this debate ; and as he had given utterance to some equivocal expressions on that subject on the occasion of its first intro-

duetion into this House-expressions which might be represented as an approval of it, if divested as it is at present of those features connected with tbe Belgian and German treaties, it was not desirable that he should interpose in the present discussion of the subject; moreover, that bis presence as a peacemaker in the county in which an election is now being run would be of infinite value to this country ; and, in view of that circumstance, and in view of those negotiations and advices, my hon. friend had prepared a discourse marked by those characteristics of mildness, and breathing that spirit of sweet reasonableness with which he so frequently delights this House; containing those very amiable references to his antagonists, those complimentary allusions to tbe lion. Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte), and those pleasant remarks as to the right hon. gentleman who leads this House, so free from anything in the nature of innuendo ; those kindly observations with reference to tbe Minister of Finance; and all suffused iu that tone of Christian charity of which he is so admirable an exponent in this House. These things were not intended for this Chamber at all, but were intended for North Bruce; but, in some way that has not been explained, but probably will be later on, the hon. gentleman's connections failed, and so lie did not get to North Bruce, whether on account of the snowstorm or for other reasons which may be supposed, and he was thrust upon this House, and was obliged to turn on the tap. He had no speech on the budget or on the preferential resolutions ; he had not prepared himself to discuss any of the questions which might legitimately come before the House; and, therefore, he was obliged to give us, very inappropriately, tbe speech which was intended for the electors of North Bruce. That is the only explanation I cau suggest for at least one of the features of the address he has given us-for the fact that in the main he steered entirely clear of the subject under discussion ; and it also illustrates the exceptionable reasonableness and sweetness of tlie discourse he gave us. I rejoice, and this House must rejoice, that we have in the public life of this country a gentleman who brings that tone into our discussions. The hon. member for Bona-venture (Mr. Marcil) desired that this should be a parliament of peacemakers. We have one of those peacemakers present ; we have had from him an illustration and an assurance of what is to come : and I trust the hon. member for Bonaventure will fold the hon. gentleman to his bosom. I must confess. Mr. Speaker, that I am very largely dependent upon tbe assurances which the hon. gentleman has himself given to ns in the course of his speech, for taking that view of his remarks ; otherwise. I would have been inclined to recall n story which was told by the late Wendell Phillips, in

connection with the anti-slavery agitation. Mr. Phillips was under the impression that the southern slaveholders, when crying out against those who were continually disturbing the peace of the country, were themselves the principal disturbers of the country's peace ; and by way of illustrating and clarifying his views, he was fond of telling a story of an old court crier who, when engaged in liis official capacity in one of the courts at Massachusetts, used to fall asleep. When the voices of the counsel who were addressing the court rose to a louder tone than usual, the crier was aroused from his slumbers, and cried out at once, ' Silence iu the court,' and immediately resumed his slumbers. This had occurred a few times, when the judge got tired of this interruption of the proceedings, and burst out in a somewhat indignant way, ' Crier, you are the only one disturbing the court, and if you will only stay asleep, there will be no more disturbance.' Iu the same way, if by some providential means, the hon. member for West York could be put into one of these slumbers which a gentleman down on Sparks street produces, I do think there would not be quite so much discord or trouble, noise, clamour and controversy as there happens to be from time to time in this community.
I endeavoured to follow the hon. gentleman in the course of his remarks last night, and I shall endeavour more or less to-day to follow them, but I am bound to say that his route was altogether too circuitous, it covered too wide a field to allow the possibility of my doing so. The discussion of all, or even one-half, of the topics the hon. gentleman saw fit to introduce in the course of his oration last night would occupy all the time at my disposal, or at the disposal of this House, from now probably until the end of the session, because there has been no subject under discussion in this parliament ever since it opened on the Gtli February last, that my hon. friend did not import into this debate. I shall therefore endeavour, not to follow him all the way round, but to confine myself as much as I possibly can to the subject immediately under discussion. My hon. friend threw absolutely no light on this subject, although he imported a great deal of heat. It was heat without light. It was certainly of no purpose for him to repeat over and over again, as he did, and as he also did last year, the platitude that it would be an excellent thing for us if we could secure free admission to Great Britain of our grain and the imposition of a hostile tariff against the grain of other countries. If we could secure admission for our grain products into the markets of the old country free of duty and have all others excluded or subjected to a discriminating, and if possible prohibitory tariff, that would be a capital thing for us. I am sure it never needed any dis-53	'
cussion or elaboration whatever to make good this contention and when the hon. gentleman repeated that platitude for the twentieth time he did not throw any light whatever on the question which this House is called upon now to consider, under the amendment of the leader of the opposition.
The hon. gentleman was asked how we could get that concession from the mother country-and that was the real point, surely, of any discussion that could be made on the subject. He was asked :	How are you
going to secure that concession ? and he answered at once : We can secure it because Mr. Chamberlain said that he was willing we should have it. Then he read-I wonder if the House will believe it without my verifying it-he actually read, in support of his statement, a paragraph from the very speech from which the right hon. leader of the House quoted the other day for the purpose of proving-as he did prove beyond all shadow of doubt-that Mr. Chamberlain had not expressed any such willingness and was entirely convinced of the impossibility of any concession of the kind being given. These were the words which my hon. friend from West York read :
Let the offer

My hon. friend did not tell us what offer it was to which Mr. Chamberlain was referring.
Let the offer, said Mr. Chamberlain, come voluntarily from them, and I believe It will be considered in this country, not in any huckstering spirit, but will be entertained as part of a greater policy intended to unite in the closest bonds of affection and interest all the communities under the British flag and all the subjects of Her Majesty throughout the empire.
Those were Mr. Chamberlain's expressions, but in that very speech my hon. friend will see, if he takes the pains to read it, and I hope he has read it-but, no, I hope he has not, because, if he has, it would be extremely disingenuous conduct on his jiart to read the passage he quoted without reading the passages in which Mr. Chamberlain pointed out the impossibility of our having any such concession made to us under the conditions existing to-day. I shall read Mr. Chamberlain's expressions, which I only repeat because it has become necessary to do so in consequence of the turn the discussion has taken and the contentions made by my hon. friend. Mr. Chamberlain was discussing three possible solutions of the question of preferential trade within the empire.
The first proposition he discussed was that the colonies should abandon their duties, which were all in the nature of protective duties more or less. He said this proposition is not a hopeful one because not one of the colonies is prepared-they are certainly not all prepared-to abandon the tariffs they now have and which involve more or less a protectionist element, more or less an element which can be used, incidentally in



some of them, purposely in others, for the protection of colonial industries. That was a proposition therefore which Mr. Chamberlain felt bound to d smiss from practical consideration. He went on to say :
There is another proposition, and that is that the colonies should keep their tariffs as they are to-day, but that the Imperial government should so arrange its tariff that a duty should be placed on foreign wheat and corn coming into the British islands, while the colonial tariffs remain as they were.
Mr. Chamberlain said no, there is no possibility of that ever being adopted. That is a result to which the workingmen of the mother country could never be induced to submit. And therefore the second proposition was dismissed as impracticable and impossible.
He said, there is a third proposition. That is the proposition of a zollverein not exactly like the German zollverein because that was a zollverein between conterminous countries, but a zollverein, with such modifications as might be capable of application to tbe condition of things in our colonies. He said that is a hopeful proposition, hut it involves the colonies abandoning all their tariff imposts which are of a protectionist character. In other words, the colonies would have to abandon all their tariff im. posts which are unlike those of tbe mother country, that is to say which either, directly and purposely, as is the case in some of the colonies, or incidentally ns is the case in * ours, involve protection to colonial industries.
The right lion, gentleman who leads the House (lit. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has shown us conclusively that it is absolutely impossible for tbe two parts of tbe resolution of my bon. friend the leader of the opposition to hang together at all, under the doctrine laid down by Mr. Chamberlain. My hon. friend insists that we must have a protective tariff applicable to the industries of this country, and in the same breath he undertakes to say that we may have that which, according to Mr. Chamberlain, is absolutely inconsistent and diametrically opposed to it, namely, a preference in the markets o'f the mother country. The right lion, the First Minister has pointed that out so conclusively and luminously that I am not going to further impose on the patience of the House by discussing a point so absolutely clear and which so entirely disposes of the resolution submitted to us by tbe leader of tbe opposition.
But tbe bon. member for West York retorts: that may be all right from our point of view, but bow is it from your point of view ? You profess that you have not a protectionist tariff, but a free trade tariff, and therefore there is no inconsistency in your going to the mother country and asking that which, it is quite evident, we would be entirely estopped from asking from the Imperial government. Well, now I want Mr. RUSSELL, (Hants).
to know who ever said we bad a free trade policy in this country. I want to know who ever said we had a free trade tariff, if I may use that expression, in this country. I do not think that anybody ever said we bad free trade in this country; I am prepared to say we do not have it.
My bon. friend has discussed this matter as if there were only two kinds of tariff, of fiscal policy, a policy of free trade, and a policy of protection. He certainly is altogether at sea when he makes a suggestion like that. We have not free trade in this country, we have not a free trade policy in this country, nor have we a protectionist policy in this country. We have in this country to-day substantially the policy with which we set out in the year 1807; that is to say, that instead of there being two kinds of fiscal policy as my hon. friend suggests, there are really three kinds, clearly and easily distinguishable. There is first of all-if I may take four or five minutes to explain a matter which is so entirely elementary-there is first of all a protectionist tariff, purposely and ostensibly framed with the object of excluding foreign goods coming from other countries, and which does exclude those products in so far as it successfully operates as a protective tariff. It is levied on goods which can be produced and which are produced in the country, and of a kind that are and can be produced in the country, levied upon them for the purpose of compelling the population to use those articles produced in the country, and for the purpose of excluding those which are produced in the foreign and competing country. That is a protectionist tariff. There is opposed to that what I may properly call a free trade tariff, such a tariff as they have in the old country, a tariff which carefully eliminates any elements of that sort, which is carefully designed for the purpose of ensuring that every penny of taxation that is paid, every penny of money taken out of the pockets of the taxpayers, is taken solely for the purpose of going into the treasury of the country. It is a tariff levied upon things, not which can be produced in the country, but which cannot by any possibility be produced in tbe country ; that I call a free trade tariff, the very opposite of the one I spoke of previously.
Then there is between these two a tariff such as we had in this country in 1867 down to the fiscal revolution of 1878, and which we are endeavouring to work our way back to, and have in a large measure worked our way back to, under tbe reformed tariff introduced by my bon. friend the Minister of Finance, a revenue tariff which is designed to exclude as far as possible the element of protection; because, as Mr. Mackenzie pointed out many years ago, in our tariff there always was an element of incidental protection, and in our tariff today there is an element of incidental

protection. But, as tlie Minister of Customs has often pointed out, that is an incident to the main purpose of the tariff, which is the collection of a revenue, and is not the protection of native industries. Now, then, this is the kind of tariff that we have to-day, and this is the kind of tariff, a revenue tariff with incidental protection, under which Mr. Chamberlain said it would be impossible for us to go to the mother country and ask for anything like a zollverein, or anything like a preference, or anything like such a scheme as is outlined in the resolution of the hon. leader of the opposition. The present tariff does afford incidental protection, that is to say, it does give a certain degree of assistance to native industries, it presents a certain obstacle to the foreign competitor, it does give a certain measure of advantage to the home producer as against the foreign competitor in the same manner as freights, insurances and other charges prevent an obstacle to the foreign competition and an advantage to the native producer. But it has for its chief purpose the collection of a revenue.
As I have said before, Mr. Chamberlain proved it impossible for us to go to the mother country and ask for preferential trade so long as we continue to maintain a tariff like that. We are prepared to stand upon that tariff, we are prepared to adhere to it. Our hon. friends opposite say it is really their own tariff, it is really their own policy, and I suppose therefore that they are also prepared to maintain and adhere to it. We all agree that it is impossible to adopt any other fiscal system or to abandon altogether all duties that could be made operative for the encouragement of native industries, and for that reason, I say again, it is absolutely impossible for my hon. friend to ask that we should accept his resolution, or to ask Mr. Chamberlain or anybody else to give us the benefit of a preferential arrangement in the English market, as matters stand at present. What may happen in the future, what may happen later on under the development of advanced Imperial ideas, what may happen in the course of a number of years, after this matter has been under consideration of the people of England and after it has been under the consideration of the people of Canada, opens up too long a vista, is too far remote for us to consider ; it is too far in the dim and distant future to be a matter of practical politics or command the consideration of practical men in a practical age, and in a businesslike parliament such as 1 understand this to be.
But my hon. friend thinks it is a very easy thing. He can make a budget for the English Chancellor of the Exchequer just as simple as rolling off a log. If you take part of the duty off tea, take a part of the duty which is now paid by the Englishman on his tea, and every penny of which goes 53}
into the treasury of the country, and put it on the competing grain coming in from the United States, you have the whole thing done in a jiffy, no difficulty about it at all. He says that when you do this the workingman of England will have to pay no more than at present, he will be simply paying the same tax as now, and you will have this brought about by one stroke of the pen, by one item in the tariff propositions in the budget speech of an English minister. Very well, just let us analyse that for a moment. Of course if the discrimination against the foreign wheat was great enough, if the tariff charge was high enough to keep it out of the English market altogether, and if we could produce enough colonial cereals to feed the population of the British isles, then it is obvious there would be no tax collected from wheat at all, no tax collected from corn ; no tax collected from grain, and the consequence would be that the English taxpayer, the English workingman would have to make up that deficit by submitting to the imposition of a direct tax. But if it did not do its perfect work, and it would not do it for it could not possibly keep out the foreign grain altogether, not for years at all events, or until we were able entirely to supply the requirements of the country, then until that tariff which my hon, friend is going to give to the British Chancellor, is imposed and does its perfect work, then there will be a certain amount of corn brought into the British islands, there will be a certain amount of corn from Canada. Well, what would be the effect of that ? The price would be raised to the English consumer. Of course that goes without saying ; and my hon. friend agrees that this duty will be paid by the English consumer. He was somewhat in doubt about that, but I think there can be no doubt about it-the duty will be paid by the English consumer. But my hon. friend says that makes no difference, because he will only be paying on his breadstuffs, the same tax that he is now paying upon tea ; that it is only as broad as it is long to him. it will make no difference to him whatever, so long as he is paying the tax. upon what article or product he is paying it. But my hon. friend forgets that apart from the duty, apart from the increment of the price that would have to be added to the foreign corn on account of the duty payable upon it. there would also be the increased price at which he would have to pay for the corn which was produced in this country. I am certain that if he makes that proposition to any intelligent workingman in the old country, he will get his answer straight from the shoulder, so clear that it will be absolutely impossible for him to misunderstand it.
Mr. Chamberlain every time that he has had occasion to discuss this question, and he has discussed it in numerous speeches- I was going to say in innumerable speeches

in the old country, he 'has discussed it in these foreign and colonial speeches that have been quoted in the debate-has presented this difficulty so straight and clear that I cannot understand how it is that my hon. friend, or any other hon. member on his side of the House who has a practical head upon his shoulders and practical sagacity and wisdom, can over and over again present this proposal which has had the bottom knocked out of it so many times. The hon. gentleman compares this case with the case of Australia. He says that the Postmaster General (Hon. Mr. Mulock) is about to go to Australia in a few days and that if he goes there he will find a country that is about to have a protective tariff imposed on it. I believe that it is likely enough that it will have. All the signs go to show that a moderate protective tariff will probably be the fiscal system of the Australian Commonwealth. He says, notwithstanding all that, are you not going to ask for a reciprocal arrangement between this country and the Commonwealth of Australia. I hope we are, and I hope, more or less confidently, that we will be able to obtain it and that by virtue of the arrangement that may be made by this government with the Australian Commonwealth a growing and profitable business may be built up between the Dominion of Canada and that new Commonwealth. My hon. friend says : If this is possible with Australasia, why not with England ? Why not ? Because there is no analogy whatever between the two cases. If Australasia were a country such as England is, a small country in its extent, or relatively so, with an enormous population, with a population of from forty to fifty millions ot' people, absolutely dependent upon their foreign trade, and upon the extent to *which they can push their manufactured products in foreign countries and obtain payment for them ; the foreign trade of which, as Mr. Chamberlain says, is the very breath of its life, and engaged in a life and death struggle with other and competing countries with enormous resources and enormous capital ; the centre of a vast and delicate financial organism which it would be fatal to disturb-if the Australasian Commonwealth presented such conditions as these, then, he would have a similar proposal to deal with to that which he is presenting to the consideration of the House and which we are asked to commend to the consideration of the British minister. The situations are so entirely different, there is such a failure of analogy between the two things that I am amazed-if I may use a word which has gone out of fashion since the leadership of the opposition has been changed-I am surprised, not to say either amazed or astounded, that either the hon. leader of the opposition, or the hon. member for West York, who has held a position in the cabinet, who has held not

only a position in the cabinet but one which brought him into close touch with questions of this character, should have presented an analogy of that sort that had no possible bearing on the question which is under deliberation by the House at the present moment.
Well, Sir, there is one other subject to which the hon. member for West York referred, and with which I will deal very briefly, the subject of bounties. He discussed the iron and steel bounties as if these bounties were being given, not for the benefit of this whole country at large, but from some partiality for the capitalists, for the individuals, and for the corporations that are engaged in the work of producing iron and steel. Was there ever a greater mistake made ? Was there ever a greater sophistry presented to the House for its consideration than that ? The hon. member the other night referred to the bounties as if there was something inconsistent between the maintenance of bounties and opposition to a protectionist system. I have always thought, and I have always said, that if there is any way at all in which it is proper for the government to grant encouragement to one industry at the expense of the general public, the peculiarly and pre-eminently proper way to do it is by means of bounties. Why ? If you pick out any particular industry and say that it is desirable and in the interest of the country at large that that industry should be established and if you set yourself to the task of establishing it and do so by means of the imposition of a protective duty, what are you doing ? You are admitting that it is a matter of consequence to the country as a whole, you are admitting that it is a matter of public interest, that it is a matter in which the whole public are concerned, or else, you have no business to be dealing with it at all. and. making that admission, you are, nevertheless, taxing the cost of establishing that industry only upon a narrowly limited circle of people who are to bear the burden of the tariff imposition which you have imposed. Is not that so ? I say it is very obvious, and af we come to the conclusion, as this country came to the conclusion years ago, that it is to the advantage of the whole Dominion that the iron and steel industry should be established, not for the benefit of the dealers in iron and steel at all, but for the benefit of the people at large, then, I say, that the peculiarly and pre-eminently proper way to do that is not by the imposition of a tariff which will be borne by a particular class, or a narrowly limited circle of people, but which will be borne by the people of the country at large and in common. Therefore, I say that there is all the difference in the world between a bounty and a protective duty for the purpose of establishing an industry, and that much can be said in favour of the granting of a bounty which
would have absolutely no application at all if one were dealing with the question of the imposition of a customs duty. That disposes then of what the hon. member for West York says in regard to lead. It may come to be considered in this country that lead is in the same position as iron and steel, that it is equally in the interest of the country to establish the lead industry, and if the government come to the conclusion that it is there will be no impropriety in granting a bounty on lead smelting, as they have granted a bounty on iron and steel production, provided that the money can he spared, because we are not bound to do two things at once. It may be very true that the lead smelters may be able to make out as perfect a case in favour of a bounty as the iron and steel men have been able to make out, and yet the government of this country may be compelled to say, under the circumstances, that they have exhausted all the surplus at their disposal, that they have pledged the resources of this country to as great an extent as they are able to do for the purpose of encouraging industries of that sort and that the lead men must bide their time. I was glad to hear the hon. Minister of Finance say that the matter had not been finally disposed of ; that it is still under consideration. I am certain that whatever resolution may be come to on the subject will be in line with the suggestions I have made and in accord with the principle to which I have just referred.
Now, I think I will not undertake to follow the hon. member for West York any further in the somewhat, if I may be permitted to say so, rambling and very circuitous route that was mapped out for us in the course of his speech on the tariff. I am certainly not going to follow him in those unamiable, unpleasant and undesirable topics which he thought it necessary to import into this debate. I have not the talent for them, I have not the genius for them, I have no liking for them, I have the most positive disgust for them, and I absolutely decline to enter into any controversies of the kind. I listened to the mover of the amendment (Mr. Borden, Halifax) with a great deal of interest to learn what it was possible for him to say in answer, as I know he must have felt, as a lawyer, it was incumbent upon him to answer, the difficulties that have been suggested from time to time, difficulties that have been so clearly presented by Mr. Chamberlain, who is his greatest friend in this matter, the greatest friend of this country, and the warmest advocate, in any exalted sphere, that has been found of the policy of a preferential tariff in favour of the products of Canada and of the colonies of the empire throughout the world. I say, that I did listen with a great deal of interest and earnestness to my hon. friend to ascertain what new thing the hon. gentleman was going to be able to say that would throw any light whatever upon this
question of the preferential tariff, which I suppose is the central feature of the resolutions which he has presented to the consideration of the House. He is a very industrious man-we all know that. And I was quite sure that if there was anything in the whole compass of literature, ancient or modern, that could be brought forward in support of his resolution, my hon. friend's industry would enable him to find it. And what did he find ? Not a single statement, I undertake to say-not a single one-of an encouraging character from any English statesman of the first rank or even of the second rank. He did not even get as much as our lamented former colleague, Mr. McNeill, who rexiresented North Bruce in the last parliament, used to get. He gave us scraps from newspapers and other periodicals. He quoted an utterance from the Saturday Review. I think one of the most encouraging of all was from a financial organ, admitting that there was a possibility that at some time in the future-twenty years from this, if I caught the phrase correctly-there might he a possibility of some change in the fiscal arrangements as now established between the mother country and the colonies. The hon. gentleman has undertaken to play the role on this question that used to be assumed by Mr. McNeill. That role is entirely unsuited to him. He is too hard-headed and practical a man to fill that role successfully-he has too much common sense and altogether too little imagination. He cannot indulge in those moonlit and mystical dreams with which the former member for North Bruce used to entertain this House. In spite of all his scraps from newspapers and his disjointed clippings from Mr. Chamberlain's speeches, though they were all patched together in a bag, he could not make the bag stand upright as the former member from North Bruce seemed to do. As hon. gentlemen will remember, it was a saying of Poor Richard, that you could not make an empty bag stand upright. This inter-imperial preferential trade bag is absolutely empty and there is not a possibility of making it stand upright. As a former Minister of Railways in this country used to remark. ' there aint nothing to it. Our friend, Mr. McNeill, used to build himself- and rightly-upon Mr. Chamberlain. And the leader of the opposition, if he has anything in this new thesis of his of Imperial preferential trade, must also build himself upon Mr. Chamberlain : because Mr. Chamberlain is the most advanced statesman in the British Empire to-day who has given the slightest encouragement to a proposition of that kind. If you do not find anything in favour of inter-imperial preferential trade in this volume (Foreign and Colonial speeches) you will look for it elsewhere in vain. Mr. Chamberlain has discussed this subject with a wideness of range, and an accuracy of detail unexcelled by any other

statesman, either Imperial or colonial. If with the genius, the ideas and the courage of William Pitt, it is impossible for Mr. Chamberlain to hold out any encouragement but such as he has given- the extent and force of which we now know, as presented by the right hon. premier yesterday-it is idle and purposeless, it is a sheer waste of time to seek for that encouragement in the utterances of any other Imperial statesman. I dismiss, therefore, that proposition, so far as it has been given us by the leader of the opposition and enforced by the hon. member for West York (Mr. Wallace) as one in which there is absolutely no substance, and upon which it is not worth our while to occupy ourselves further under the present circumstances of the country.
But there is another* element in the hon. gentleman's resolution, another article in this new opposition' creed. I believe they are revising their creed, as the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) said the other night that his church were revising theirs.
Somebody else ought to do the same.

We are always ready to revise our creed when good reasons can be shown for it. I refer now to the last branch of the resolution, the proposal, if I understand it aright, that we should retaliate on all countries that do not treat us fairly :
This House is further of opinion that equivalent or adequate duties should be imposed by Canada upon the products and manufactures of countries not within the empire in all cases where such countries fail to admit Canadian products and manufactures upon fair terms, and that the government should take for this purpose all such available measures as may be found necessary.
We are asked by this resolution to retaliate in all cases. Yet, if I understood the remarks of the leader of the opposition, he was going to except from it our great neighbour, the United States, which certainly does not treat us with that degree of fairness, or generosity, at any rate, in the matter of tariff regulations, which we might reasonably expect. He is going to except the United States and apply the resolution to Germany, and to Germany alone. Now, one word as to retaliation. Of course, the temptation to retaliate when injured is one of the first instincts of our brute nature. We instinctively resort to the lex talionis which demands an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth. But while the first impulse, the brute instinct of the natural man is to retaliate, the civilized man pauses to reflect. He does not obey his immediate impulse. He first asks himself the question whether he is likely to accomplish by retaliation any useful purpose. Now, I think I can suggest why the hon. leader of the opposition excepted the United States, not in

the terms of his resolution, but by his comments, from the intended operation of this principle of retaliation. We did retaliate on the United States some years ago. Our policy of 1S78 was professedly founded, in part, upon the idea of retaliating upon the United States-of giving the United States, as It was pleasantly put, that sin-cerest form of flattery which consists in imitation-we would retaliate upon them for their conduct towards us almost continuously in recent years. But what did we get for our retaliation ? What was the consequence of our national policy ? Why, I do not need to refer to any higher authority than the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell), who addressed us the other day, for any answer to that question. He described the consequences very eloquently, indeed, very forcibly. It led to a condition of things in this country which was anything but pleasant for us, a condition of things under which we were losing our population, a condition of things so entirely the reverse of prosperous, that he could see no remedy but reversion on the part of this country to the principle of free trade. So, I suppose, this is the reason why we are not asked to retaliate against the United States.
Coming for a time to the remarks which the hon. member for Pictou addressed to the House, I was struck, as other hon. gentlemen must have been, with the fact that two speeches-I trust I shall not he considered presumptuous if I say twro excellent speeches-one by the hon. member for Pictou, and one by the hon. member for South Wentworth (Mr. Smith), were entirely destructive of each other on some of the main contentions presented to the House. It occurred to me that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden (Halifax), with his keen perception for logical fallacies ; with- his strong, clear and logical brain, must have reflected when he heard these gentlemen ; How happy could I be with either were the other fair charmer away. Each of these supporters of his made a good speech, but the speech of one, to a large extent, nullified the speech of the other. The thought occurred to me at first that these two gentlemen could not have consulted together before taking such divergent views on the preferential tariff, but on reflection it seemed more probable that they did compare notes. They had instructions from their leader of course to oppose the preferential tariff. This was common ground. But they must not both oppose it on the same grounds. The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell) was retained to oppose the preferential tariff on the ground that it was going to interfere witli our manufacturing industries, and the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Smith) was retained to oppose it on the ground that it was not really a preference at all, and that it did not do any good to the people of the mother country. And so the hon. gentleman from Pictou (Mr. Bell), I
presume, said to tlie hon. member for Wentworth : You know there are many Imperialists in Canada and there is a strong British feeling which heartily welcomed and cordially supports the preferential tariff, so you tell the people of the country, through the House of Commons, that this tariff makes no concessions whatever to the mother country, and that before the government brought in this tariff, which professes to give concessions to Great Britain, they took good care to raise the general tariff on the articles to which the preference would apply, and to raise it so high that the preference was only such in name, and no benefit was left to the mother land. And then said the hon. member (Mr. Bell) : I will play on the other string ; there are a lot of manufacturers in Canada who are nervous about their gains. They are afraid that they will not have such an easy time during the next few years as they have had in the past, and so I will say : This preferential tariff gives such concessions to the people of Great Britain that it is going to ruin the industries of Canada. And so these two hon. gentlemen played their two discordant tunes, the speech of the one completely nullifying the speech of the other. Which is right? My hon. friend from Pictou belauded the men who introduced the national policy in 1878. These, he said, were men of blood and iron like Bismarck, and they went on with their task without sentimental considerations. These were the men, quoth he, who said : If this tariff is not good for British connection, then so much the worse for British connection. These were the men who said : Driven out of the markets of the civilized world, the mother land is compelled to force her wares upon savages at the point of the bayonet. They did not allow any sentimental considerations to interfere with the maintenance of the industries of Canada, as this government has done by its preferential tariff. This was the drift of his reference to the subject. He argued that the time was coming when, in consequence of the concessions given to the manufacturers of Great Britain by this preferential tariff, many of the manufacturers of Canada would be driven out of existence. His remarks were quoted by the right hon. the Prime Minister the other day, and in consequence I need not make a more explicit reference. But look at what the member for Wentworth (Mr. Smith said, and you will find that he took an entirely different tack. He says :
I can gather no inference from the figures I have quoted but that the preference we have given to Great Britain only places her on a par with or in a worse condition than the United States, because before this preference was given hon. gentlemen opposite raised the duties to a large extent on the class of goods we import from Great Britain.
We, therefore, see that these two followers of tlie leader of the opposition, speaking in
this House on the same day and on the same subject, give such diametrically opposite views as to the operation of the preferential tariff, that it is absolutely impossible for a plain man like myself to know what to think about the matter at all. They presented the same differences of opinion in regard to details that they presented in regard to the main issue. The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell) said that relatively, under the operation of the preferential tariff, the trade of England had increased as compared with the trade of the United States and of other countries ; while the hon. gentleman from Wentworth (Mr. Smith) proved to his own satisfaction that England did not hold her own in the Canadian market with either the United States or Germany, in spite of the preferential tariff. What can a plain man who sits here at the feet of these oracles for the purpose of learning the truth, what can he believe in view of this divergence of opinion between them. All that is left for me to do is to go to the trade returns, and there I find, and I am bound to make the admission, that the trade of the old country, even under the preferential tariff, has not been able to hold its own relatively with the trade of the United States or of Germany ; certainly not relatively with the trade of the United States. But, supposing that to be true, what is the vital question which remains to be answered ? If in spite of the preferential tariff that we have given Great Britain ; if notwithstanding that the United States and Germany are handicapped by a tariff discrimination against them ; if in spite of that handicap in favour of the old country she has still a life and death struggle to preserve her own in our markets against the United States, is it not a vital question for Englishmen to ask themselves : Where would we have been were It not for that preferential tariff ? Surely the response to this question is a conclusive answer to the argument, that we have done England no good by the enactment of our preferential tariff. This much, at all events, we have succeeded in doing. If you look at the actual importation of dutiable goods, you 'will find that they reached the nadir point in 1897. You will find that the importation of dutiable goods from Great Britain to Canada reached absolutely its lowest figure in 1897, and since that it has been absolutely upon the ascending scale-I do not say relatively to other countries, hut I do say that it has been on the ascending scale since 1897. If you look further to what is a more interesting set of figures than this ; if you look at the percentage of imports from England and the United States, and take the percentage of the dutiable to the total imports-the percentage of dutiable goods that we get from Great Britain compared to our total dutiable importations into the country, and the percentage we get from the United States of duti-

able goods compared to the total dutiable goods imported into this country, you 'will find this very striking fact to be demonstrated, that we began in 1867 with nearly 65 per cent of our whole dutiable imports from Great Britain and only about 23 per cent from the United States, and that ratio has been continually declining as against Great Britain and continually ascending as in favour of the United States ever since the year 1867 down to and until the year 1897, when the percentage of dutiable goods imported from Great Britain went down to 30J per cent, and the percentage of dutiable goods imported from the United States ascended to 46 per cent and a fraction. So that down to 1897, our percentage of dutiable goods from the old country was continually declining and our percentage of dutiable goods from the United States was continually ascending. Then, if you examine the figures of 1898,' 1899, and 1900, you will find-and you may attribute it to whatever you please-I attribute it to the preferential tariff-that the declining ratio in one column and the ascending ratio in the other column were arrested in the year 1897. I think that is a conclusive demonstration of the operation of the preferential tariff-not as conclusive a demonstration as we would like to see of its operation in favour of the old country, but proving conclusively that it has operated in favour of the old country and that but for its operation the declining ratio I spoke of would have been reduced to zero and there would have been hardly any proportion of dutiable goods imported from Great Britain into this country at all. Well Sir, what does all this prove ? If it be true' as my hon. friend from West York and other bon. gentlemen opposite have said, that in spite of the preferential tariff England is not holding her own in our markets with the United States or with Germany what does it all prove ? It proves what Lord Rosebery discovered, and told the English people in solemn tones the other day, that they are at this moment engaged in a hand-to-hand and life-and-death struggle with the people of the United States and the people of Germany.
Hear, hear; free trade against protection, and the protectionists will win out.

What I say is, if, considering the position we hold towards the mother country, and considering all that the mother country has done for us, we are not prepared, when we can do so without detriment to ourselves, and even though it were as we contend that it is not with detriment to ourselves, to give the mother country a preference, I want to know what sort of Canadians we would be if we had not a strong impulse to assist the mother country in that hand-to-hand struggle to preserve her trade from the incursions of com-Mr. RUSSELL (Hants).
petition from the United States and Germany.
My hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Bell) complained that there was no originality or inventiveness in this government, and no originality or inventiveness displayed by the Finance Minister in his budget speech or in his tariff. Well, Sir, whatever complaints might be made of the hon. gentleman himself. I think no one will deny to him the merit of originality and inventiveness. He has invented a variety of fictions, which he presented to us the other day. The first he invented was as to the permanence and stability of the Tory tariff. Assuredly that was an invention, or at least a discovery- that the tariff which existed in this country from 1879 down to 1897 was a permanent tariff. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance very properly claims as a merit of the tariff that was enacted in 1897, that it has remained on the statute-book ever since practically without any change [DOT]whatever-I believe absolutely without a single change ; so that merchants and manufacturers know what they have to depend on, and can make their arrangements accordingly. My friend Mr. McClure, who was in this House last session, showed me the changes which were made by the Conservative party in their tariff, and they ran up into the hundreds. I fail to remember accurately the very groat number of changes that had been made in this permanent and inelastic tariff, which was introduced In 1879, and the permanence and stability of which has been the discovery of my hon. friend from Pictou.
Another discovery wTiich my hon. friend has made is that of the grievance on the Bart of the wool men. Now, I have looked through our tariff to find out what grievance the man who deals in wool has. The hon. gentleman suggests that it is wrong to encourage the manufacturers of the old country by placing a burden upon some particular class of people in this country ; and the particular class of people in this country upon whom among others he says we have placed a burden by the preferential tariff are the men interested in the manufacture of wool. Now, I am not very much of a hand at tariffs
Hear, hear.

That is correct; I am like my hon. friend the leader of the opposition -this is not my trade. I have heard a story told, I think of Richard Brinsley Sheriden, that he was coming home from his club one night a little under the influence of a certain kind of excitement to the physical and nervous system, when he saw a friend of his lying in the gutter slightly inebriated. With the instinct of humanity, the returning club man tried to lift his friend out of the gutter, but found that it was absolutely impossible to do so: so he said, ' My good friend, I cannot lift you out, but I will do the next best thing-I will
lie down beside you.' My hon. friend the leader of the opposition is not an expert in tariffs any more than I am. I would be 'glad to help him out of his scrapes; but as 1 cannot do that, I will do the next best thing-I will get in alongside of him.
But 1 can read common ordinary print, and I looked at this customs tariff in the Canadian Parliamentary Guide and scanned it carefully with the purpose of finding out what is the peculiar and special grievance under which the dealers in wool and the manufacturers of woollen goods are labouring. And so far as I understand, every one of them is put on the* highest ad valorem tariff which is to be found in the whole list. 1 cannot find one of them under 35 per cent ad valorem, from which, If you deduct the one-third preferential rate, you get down to 23 per cent. And, looking at the figures presented a year ago by the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson), I find that, averaging the importations of wool into this country, they were the highest in the whole list. So that these people stand in our tariff in the most favoured position, and if there is any protection in this tariff-and I have admitted that incidentally there is-they get the fullest benefit of it. If there is any discrimination at all, it is in their favour, because they are put on the highest scale, and besides, they have, as others have, the freights and the insurance in their favour, and all the other obstacles which foreign competitors have to encounter. And. if, in addition to all that, they want something *which nobody else has in this country, it 1s absurd to talk of their being subject to 'any exceptional burden. The case is just the opposite. It is the case of a particular class of people.asking that we should burden all the rest of the community in their favour. My hon. friend must perceive that, I am sure he sees it. and I shall not waste time by discussing the point any further.
The hon. gentleman made another discovery and one which is greatly to the credit of the present Finance Minister. He discovered that twenty years ago-quite a long period in the history of a ministry or the history of a man-twenty years ago there was a Finance Minister in this country who was as good as the one who now administers our financial affairs.
A great deal better.

My hon. friend has discovered that there was a better Finance Minister, but he has not discovered that ever since Sir Leonard Tilley's day down to the present administration, there was another Finance Minister in that whole period of twenty years worth mentioning at all. He has to go back all of twenty years to find any Finance Minister who can at all compare with my hon. friend who now controls that department. I say that that is a high compliment to jiay to my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding), but it is not a high compliment to pay to the hon. gentleman who filled that position in the late government (Mr. Foster). I know that the ex-Finance Minister is not a persona grata to the hon. gentlemen on the other side. We do not often hear his name ; they never speak of him. But to return to Sir Leonard Tilley twenty years ago. Twenty years is a long time, half the time that the children of Israel were wandering in the wilderness. These hon. gentlemen are fond of going back to history. I remember that when Mr. Foster went down to the town of New Glasgow to deliver a speech in my hon. friend's (Mr. Bell) own riding in my hon. friend's interest-and I think that when Mr. Foster put himself out so much to accommodate my hon. friend, the hon. gentleman might have had some kind words to speak of him in this House-when Mr. Foster went to Pic-tou to deliver a discourse, which, I think, was entitled a discourse to the young men about to enter on their political studies- a discourse addressed to the callow fledglings of the Tory nest down in the town of New Glasgow-all his address was occupied with historical reminiscences. These hon. gentlemen all go back to history, no doubt for the reason that the best part of the Conservative party is underground. Its best part is historical, and the only life it has left is its historical life. Its epitaph has come to be written. There was a story told of two gentlemen who were discussing the rival merits of New York and Philadelphia.
Dispense.

I do not know whether the story is worth telling or not, but I tell it, not for the intrinsic merit it may have, but because of its applicability to the situation. After each one had cited the merits of his native city, the Philadelphian made his final boast that the Quaker City was better laid out than New York. Well, retorted the Now Yorker, when New York is as dead as Philadelphia it will be just as well laid out. Well, Mr. Speaker, whenever the Liberal party is as dead in this country as the Conservative party, we expect it to make as comely a corpse and hope it may have a more creditable history.
My hon. friend, referring to this great Finance Minister who existed twenty years ago, said that Sir Leonard Tilley had so managed the finances of his day that lie reduced the net debt of Canada from $3(5.17 per head to $35.75 per head, and the net interest from $1.61 to $1.50 per head, thus diminishing the annual impost on every individual by 14 cents. And contrasting that with the performance of the present Finance Minister, he said that the debt had increased from $153.33 per head, which it was when the late government left office, to $64.75 per head, and the net interest from $1.42 to $1.78. But the point on which I would desire enlightenment Is how it came to pass that this debt, which Sir Leonard

Tilley had reduced to $35.75 per head twenty-years ago had been increased to $03.33 per head by his successors among hon. gentlemen opposite ? Why is this thus ? Of course, it must be due to the bad management of those incompetent Finance Ministers which these hon. gentlemen had as successors to Sir Leonard Tilley. Surely if it was a great credit to Sir Leonard Tilley that he reduced the debt to $35.75 per head, it is a great shame to his successors that they should have increased it so prodigiously and rapidlv to $63.33.
Mr. Foster used to understand this matter pretty thoroughly, and I spent considerable time last year over his speech on this very subject. He made a far better presentment to the House than any of these hon. gentlemen opposite have made this session, and when X contrast Mr. Foster's effort with theirs I can realize how they must have sighed :
For the touch of a vanished hand,
And the sound of a voice that is still.
I can appreciate their feelings when they came to discuss the finance question and had to come from the Hon. George Eulas Foster down to

I pause. I have no desire to say anything that could by any possibility be considered as unpleasant. But Mr. Foster made this calculation-a calculation more favourable to the Conservative party, I am bound to say, than the hon. member for Pictou made in regard to the debt. It is common ground, however, that the debt during the eighteen years of Conservative rule had been increased $118,000,000. My hon. friend (Mr. Bell, Pictou) made it out to be increased very much more than that, but he was several millions mistaken-it was only increased $118,000,000. But Mr. Foster said : It was all right to increase our debt by I that enormous figure, because we were building our house and had to incur large capital expenditure. He went into the expenditures for which this debt had been incurred, and showed to his own satisfaction that they amounted to $142,000,000. He said : There is what you have to show for your debt. It is true you have a mortgage of $118,000,000, but look at the splendid edifice we have put up for you. Then he went on to contrast the capital expenditures under Liberal rule, and showed that we had only made a capital expenditure amounting to $11,000,000. But Mr. Foster did not attempt to draw any conclusion from what he had said, nor did my hon. friend on the other side. When I was at school, I used to study the rule of three, and my hon. friend, no doubt, did the same. The method, as he will remember, was to multiply the second and third terms together and divide by the first. Calculating according to that rule you will find what debt would have been put upon the country had the same ratio as under Conserva-Mr. RUSSELL (Hants).
tive rule been maintained. And, if you work it out you will find that, according to the highest financial authority that ever sat on the other side during the Liberal regime, in proportion to our capital expenditures we added less to the debt than did the Conservative government. If you put $142,000,000 as the first term, $118,000,000 as the second term, and $11,000,000 as the third term, and work it out, you will see that we had a right to impose a debt of $9,102,008 before we could be called to account by those who favoured this expenditure by the Conservatives. And we did not impose any such debt upon the people. My hon. friend himself states the amount at $7,000,000. As a matter of fact, I believe it was stated last year allowing for about $2,500,000 used to pay floating debts of the previous administration at only $5,250,000. I care not what figure you take-as I have already said, I have no skill in figures. But in any case whether you take the larger or the lower figure we are some millions of dollars within the debt we would have a right to pile up against the people of this country before our record could fairly be challenged by those who approved of the record of Conservative rule.
Now, there was one other discovery the hon. gentleman made, but it is so stale and so hackneyed and shop-worn that I am almost ashamed to allude to it. That was the statement that we had blundered into the preferential tariff, that we did not know anything about the German and Belgian treaties, that we constructed our preferential tariff in such a way as to run up against these treaties without knowing they were there. If there was an intelligent schoolboy of ten years of age who did not know all about these German and Belgian treaties, he ought to have been whipped. Surely, every one in this country knew about these treaties; and nothing could be clearer than that the administration and the leader of the government knew what was to be encountered in connected with them. They not only knew, but calculated upon it. As has been explained ad nauseam, they said :	We will
take chances. We shall never get rid of these restrictions upon the commercial freedom of the empire until we challenge these treaties and have the matter fought out. They framed their preferential tariff with that idea implicitly contained in it if not explicitly stated, and they fought the matter out. I shall not waste the time of the House by going into a long discussion over that. Everybody knows that it was this expedient and this expedient alone that led to the abolition of these restrictions on the commercial freedom of the British Empire. The hon. gentleman tells us that the seeds were sown by Sir Charles Tupper in the various interviews he had with the Imperial government and the articles he pub-
lislied in tlie Nineteenth Century and the London magazines. Well, as the right lion, premier said last year of some other seeds sown by the former leader of the Opposition, these seeds were absolutely sterile ; They never produced any result. It was only when this government took issue with the Imperial government and compelled the consideration of the subject that the result was	brought about.
And when the measure was brought down, we were told that it was absolutely impossible to bring about that result. But it was brought about, and it was by no other agency than the introduction of the preferential tariff of this country. I will simply read one short historical review In the London Times of 1897-and with that I will take my seat-for the purpose of showing that this measure and this alone was the cause of the abolition of this restriction upon the commerce of the empire. This was written not during the controversy, but when that controversy was cold and dead, and when the writer could review it with the knowledge and impartiality of the historian :
The Dominion parliament met on March 28, and on St. George's day, April 23, a tariff Bill was introduced, of which the effect was speedily felt throughout the empire. The principal feature of the Bill was that it adopted one tariff as the general tariff of the Dominion and another preferential tariff for those countries which showed a desire to trade with Canada upon terms of reciprocal commercial advantage. Whatever the duties imposed by the general tariff, the duties of the preferential tariff should be reduced in proportion to them for one year by 12i per cent and after one year, by 25 per cent. As Great Britain and the British colony of New South Wales were at the time of the introduction of the tariff the only communities trading on the required terms with Canada, the tariff Bill became in effect a Bill for the preferential treatment of British trade.
Surely this is an answer to the remarks made on the other side of the House on this subject.
The Bill, which was received with enthusiasm in this country, gave rise to a keen discussion as to the power of the colonial government under the existing treaties of Britain with Germany and Belgium to extend to the mother country any commercial advantages which was not given to these countries, and to all others having a claim to the most-favoured nation treatment. Legal authorities in this country were understood to hold the view that the treaties did, as a matter of fact, preclude all British colonies from giving to Great Britain preferential advantage over most-favoured foreign nations, and to that extent constituted an interference with the fiscal freedom of the empire. The theory of the matter was not put to the test of authoritative decision. In recognition of the strong public feeling which existed on the subject, the treaties were denounced in July, and an irksome barrier to the possible commercial union of the empire was thus, on the initiative of Canada, removed.
Sir, this is absolutely conclusive that if , we are now in a position in which we can,
with any possibility of success, approach the question of inter-imperial preferential trade, the fact that we are in that position is exclusively due to the proceedings taken by this government on St. George's day, L897.

That it is highly desirable that the largest possible freedom of commercial intercourse should obtain between the Dominion of Canada and the United States, and that it is expedient that all articles manufactured in or natural products of either of the said countries, should he admitted free of duty into the ports of the other. That it is further expedient that the government of the Dominion should take steps at an early date to ascertain on what terms and conditions arrangements can be effected with the United States for the purpose of securing full unrestricted reciprocity of trade therewith.
I would like to ask hon. gentlemen opposite: which of these policies do they adhere to ? in Canada compete with the United States V 1 have invariably answered : Yes, we can on equal terms, but not in the ratio of seventy millions of people to six millions, not when we are handicapped. Therefore, I say that the question is irrelevant, that it does not cover the case and that the question should not be considered from that standpoint. since July, 1S67, the united foreign commerce of the provinces has arisen from an annual average for thirteen years before confederation of 1)00,000 to the enormous amount in the seventh year after confederation of $210,000,000.
The Hon. George Brown in these words refers to the importance of our interprovincial traffic, and he also indicates taut wnen we have prosperous interprovincial traffic we also have large exports and imports. I desire to say, Mr. Speaker, that there is no class of people in this country who have applied themselves more diligently to their business and more faithfully to the task set before them of studying new process for creating new enterprises than have the manufacturers of Canada. I therefore repeat what I said in opening, that the language which has been used by some hon. gentlemen opposite in regard to our manufacturers is unworthy of being heard in this parliament. 1 believe, Sir, that we ought to encourage in every way possible the manufacturers of this country in their efforts to give employment to our people in all legitimate enterprises.
Now, Sir, as to this matter of preferential trade which has been spoken of time and again in this House, and in connection with which the right hon. the Prime Minister and the Finance Minister referred to what had taken place at a meeting of the Chambers of Commerce in London last summer. Mr. Fielding) told us that the only important matter in reference to preferential trade that had occurred recently took place at the meeting of the 4th Congress of the Chamber of Commerce in London last year, and in view of what has been said upon that question, I think it well to correct the statements made by hon. gentlemen opposite lest they should create a false impression abroad. It is a very easy task for a member to get up in this House and tell of the difficulties in the way of securing preferential trade within the empire, but it is a very difficult task to bring forward a scheme which will remove these difficulties, and which would be in the line of what I might call constructive politics. I may state that the Rt. Hon. Joseph Chamberlain was honorary chairman of the Congress of the Chambers of Commerce which met in London in 1896, but owing to his numerous duties and to the fact that the Imperial parliament was in session he was unable to occupy that position last year. Extracts from the speech of Mr. Chamberlain in 1896 have been read, and I may be pardoned if I present to the House a few of the utterances of Lord Selborne. I quote from his speech :

There has been more assertion of dogma in this question of free trade and protection than ever has been current among theologians. I believe free trade not to be a religion, but to be a policy.
Again, in speaking of the difficulties which had been overcome in bringing about the federation of the different Australian colonies, he said :
In Australia difficulties have been overcome, and therefore it does seem to me that, probably .in a different way, they may be also overcome in the empire. Union in any political sense is one of the problems of the future.
The lit. Hon. C. T. Ritchie, who was then president of the British Board of Trade, and who is now the Home Secretary, said on that occasion :
I hope Australia will follow the example of Canada and do what she can to promote British trade. We also hope that this is only the beginning of some closer commercial action in the future. I myself believe that the days of the strict Manchester free trade school are passing away.

I would like to ask hon. gentlemen opposite if there, are any improvements they have made in the transportation facilities that have given the producers of this country any cheaper freight rates than existed when they came into power ? be a matter of local importance, but it is one of very wide importance as well-we have repeatedly urged the improvement of the harbour of Toronto in such a way as to allow the vessels of 14 feet draught, that use the St. Lawrence canals, to be able to come into the harbour ; we have shown that Toronto is a great distributing centre, that more freight tonnage comes into and goes out of Toronto than comes into and goes out of Montreal ; and yet we cannot get the government to move in this matter. We find all kinds of policies in regard to transportation, we find expenditures in all parts of the country, and yet the centre of the part of the Dominion where the exports are produced, and where they are gathered for export, is left without necessary improvements. There is another feature of the transportation problem, and one that I referred to a few days ago. That is, what I might almost call the calamity to the St. Lawrence route, of the transference by the Grand Trunk Railway of its terminus from Montreal to Portland. I do not know what the opinion of other members of the House may be with regard to this question, nor do I care. When I referred to it the other day, I was accused by the Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) with introducing politics into the discussion of this question. I should be sorry to create such a precedent. But, I venture to say that the very liberal manner in which the government dealt with the Grand Trunk Railway when it took over the Drummond
County Railway, had the effect I said it had. Calculated at 34 per cent, the payments by the government of $140,000 a year, and $500,000 given to assist them in Improving Victoria bridge, was in effect, a payment to the Grand Trunk Railway of $4,500,000, and this money the Grand Trunk Railway used to side-track Montreal, and to make Portland in the United States their terminus. I say that the government, when the Grand Trunk Railway stated publicly that their policy was to make Portland their terminus in summer as well as winter, should have inserted in their bargain a condition that would not tolerate that sort of thing, and I believe they could have prevented it.
Now, what do we find in the discussion of this transportation question ? Let me remind the House that every steamer that loads and unloads In Montreal, employs in labour and in the purchase of supplies for that purpose a sum of between $4,000 and $5,000; and the men who do that work come from various places down the St. Lawrence to work on the docks in Montreal, and the money is distributed among them. I say therefore, that instead of these men earning that money, it will be earned by aliens if the Grand Trunk make their terminal in the United States, as they intend to do. The government could have prevented this misfortune, and in neglecting to do so they have not shown ordinary business foresight. We have lost the German market, and we are not getting other markets which I think we should have. Now. Sir, we are sending to France only $1,372,359, while we are taking from France $4,464,938. eral election. I remember when the right hon. gentleman came to Toronto to address our people on political questions, and when he was so well received. I think I express the sentiments fairly of this side of the House when I say, that, apart from the remarks of the hon. leader of the opposition himself, the discussion of this question by hon. members opposite has given rise to no slight feeling of disappointment, a disappointment which has arisen from the manner of discussion, from the criticism and the manner of criticism, because, hon. gentlemen seem to have failed in raising this discussion to anything like the level of a budget debate, to anything like the traditional dignity and importance of such a debate.
