The disjointed and apparently aimless criticism which has been indulged in by some lion, gentlemen opposite has upset all the preconceived ideas of some of us as to what a budget debate ought to be, to the ideas which were formed, not by actual participation in such a discussion, but more from the pages of parliamentary history in Great Britain, or from the pages of parliamentary history in our own country-from the pages of parliamentary history in Great Britain from the days when the Great Commoner assailed the budgets of the administration of a Walpole, or later on, when the younger Pitt, Canning, Burke, and Fox, did not think it beneath their dignity to give their best time and their best thought to the discussion of the principles of finance. It was on the occasion of the budget debate that these principles were discussed, and not mere petty details. Later still, when men of the stamp of Sir Robert Peel, and Lord Derby and Richard Cobden and John Bright, gave their time to the discussion of the financial policy of their country, they employed their best thought and effort in elevating the debate. Throughout the past century and a half at least of British history, the occasion of the budget debate has been an occasion for the discussion of broad financial principles, and not the discussion of mere petty details, and also, I think, it has been so in our own House. We may go back to the days of confederation, we may pass onward from that time until twenty-four years ago, when the late Rt. Hon. Sir John Macdonald moved his celebrated resolution in this House, known as the national policy resolution. While we may disagree as to the principle of that resolution which he then moved, we agree that his resolution was one which Involved the discussion of a broad principle. It was a discussion worthy of the occasion, and so it has been down through succeeding years in budget debate. Hon. members who then occupied the opposition benches discussed the question from the standpoint of financial principles. So it has been through succeeding years, right down, one might also say, to the present year of grace when we were treated, not to a dis-
cussion of these broad principles, hut to a rambling discussion of the details of government, covering almost the whole of this vast country. Having these matters before us, is it any wonder that we did suffer a little disappointment on this side of the House when we noticed lion, members opposite, in their discussion and in their criticism, degenerating into the merest kind of commonplace, what, all our preconceived notions led us to look forward to as a veritable battle of giants. I am free to admit that it may be to some extent my own lack of information in regard to the details of the finances of this country which has rendered me incapable of appreciating either the force or object of the criticism which has been levelled at the present financial statement. I have not been able to make up my mind whether the object of the critic was to detract from the credit which is due properly to the hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) for his admirable financial statement, or whether the real object was one of self-indulgence, of a little self-glorification over some real or imaginary achievement which took place in the early days of the Conservative party. If the object of hon. gentlemen be the first of these at which I have hinted, namely, to detract from the credit which is due the government for their statement as to the finances of Canada, the weakness of the assault which they were able to make has only served to magnify the exceptionally strong position which the government is able to occupy upon that subject, but, if, on the other hand, their object be merely self-glorification over their own greatness of years ago. I am sure that every one in this House will admit that it is the prescriptive and undoubted right of an opposition to extract all the consolation it can from the memory of vanished greatness. But, there is a limit to all things, a line must be drawn, and the time comes when the House demands something more substantial than reminiscences of the last fifteen, or twenty, or twenty-five years.
I believe I have the right to inquire : Upon wliat principle this question is being discussed by hon. gentlemen opposite. If a principle at all is involved ; what is the principle ? Do they charge that the government in its past management of the finances of this country or in its proposals for the future, has violated some recognized economic principle ? If so, what is the principle that has been violated ? Do they charge that the government in its management of the finances has committed some fundamental error ? Then, what is the error ? Do they charge that the government has been reckless and extravagant or worse ? If that be the charge, then, as a matter of common justice, the government is entitled to have the charge laid in detail in order to be able to meet it. But, failing any charge of that kind, failing any criticism upon any principle, economic! or otherwise, is it to be wondered at that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright), as far back as Friday last, threw out a mild hint in this House that if hon. gentlemen opposite had nothing more substantial to offer in discussion than had been contributed up to that time, the debate might as well be brought to a close because further discussion was not only unnecessary but a positive waste of the time of the House. There is no doubt in my mind that the timely hint from the hon. minister (Sir Richard Cartwright) was an incentive to the bon. leader of the opposition to put forth some effort to rescue his followers from the humiliating position which they were likely to occupy, and as a result of that effort we have the amendment which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden) saw fit to move. It would be charitable to say that that amendment is a creature of unfortunate circumstances. It is a sort of emer

gency ration which the leader of the opposition has laid before the House. No one can claim that it is an amendment born of any present financial condition in Canada, or justified by any trade condition now existent. When I read the first clause of that amendment I was struck with the idea that the draughtsman, by the language which he had employed, had gone beyond any meaning which he himself intended to convey. But when we remember that the draughtsman was none other than the leader of the opposition himself whose practice of the legal profession has long accustomed him to the use of language, and the use of it precisely and concisely ; we must conclude that the language of the amendment probably expresses his own ideas upon the subject. In order that we may understand each other the better, let us examine that first clause. Does it mean, as I believe it means, that there is not sufficient or adequate protection in Canada to-day ? Does the hon. gentleman mean by the words 'pronounced protection' that the tariff now in force does not afford sufficient protection ? If that is his meaning we can argue it upon that hypothesis. Is it the insinuation of the language he has used that there is not sufficient assurance or encouragement to industries in this country. If that be the meaning we can argue it upon that hypothesis. Certain it is that if such be the real meaning of the first clause of the amendment, it is nothing less than an absolute refutation of the statements made by him and by his followers in this House and in the country. Is it not a fact that for the past four years the Conservatives have charged that the tariff which is in force to-day is what they call the grand old national policy ? Has it not been charged by the gentlemen opposite in this very debate, that the tariff now in force is a thoroughly protective policy? Has it not been charged on the platform and in the press, that the Liberals were unable or unwilling to make a

tariff of their own and that they boldly adopted the tariff of the Conservative party? Do we not remember those stories about the stolen clothes ? Was our memory not refreshed a few days ago by the reference of the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell) to the footpad and the stolen purse. Has it not been the whole claim of the Conservative party up to the time this amendment was moved, that the present tariff in Canada is the tariff inaugurated by the Conservative party and is a protective tariff. Well, if it be correct that it is a protective tariff and that the Conservatives are responsible for it, is it not reasonable to suppose that they thought it adequate and sufficient when they brought it into being and kept it in force so long ?
But, Sir, there is a wide difference of opinion upon the question of the tariff in this country, though it may be that the difference perhaps is more over a name or over language than over any real matter of greater account. I believe that with very slight change in the language of clause one this amendment could be made such a one as would commend itself to the judgment of every hon. member in this House. Strike out, if you will, the words 'pronounced protection,' which are objectionable to members on this side of the House. Do not say that we have a revenue tariff as we claim on this side and do not say that it is a protective tariff, as is claimed on the other, but merely make your amendment to read : That by the continuance of the present tariff policy adequate protection is given to the industries of Canada ; and then you will have a fair expression of the best opinion of hon. members on both sides regarding the tariff. I do not know that anything in the politics of the country has ever been so persistently and so inconsistently misrepresented as the position of the Liberal party upon the question of the tariff. Hon. members opposite surely must know better than they say in regard to this. Hon. members opposite surely by this time have learned what is the Liberal position upon the question of the tariff. T did not know that the Liberal tariff policy went back as far as confederation, but I have heard to-day that ever since the year of confederation the policy of the Liberal party upon the question of the tariff has been, that we should have a tariff but it should be a tariff of revenue. We on this side of the House realize that we require a certain amount of money each year to conduct the affairs of the country. For the coming year it is to be about $46,000,000, but every year a large amount of money must be provided and the simple question is : How is that money going to be raised ?
There are various methods of raising money for national purposes. It might be raised by the imposition of a direct tax ; it might be raised in other ways ; but the policy of the Liberal party and the present Mr. GUTHRIE.
government is that the money necessary to be raised each year to conduct the affairs of the government shall be raised by means of a tariff, and that tariff shall be so adjusted as to produce sufficient revenue. That was the policy of the Liberal party away back in 1872. It was the policy of the administration of the late Alexander Mackenzie, and in the closing years of that administration, at a time when there was not enough revenue to meet the requirements of the public expenditure, it was proposed to increase the tariff-why ? Not certainly for the reason suggested by hon. gentlemen opposite, in order that a certain degree of protection might be given, but solely to provide the Finance Minister with sufficient revenue'to carry on the affairs of the country. That was the policy of the Liberal party then, and when they went out of power in 1878 they did not change their policy. In succeeding years the policy of the Liberal party on the tariff was the same. They said, we will maintain a tariff, but it will be a tariff for revenue and not for protection. The hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Kemp) quoted some articles on unrestricted reciprocity. It is true, at one time the Liberal party did advocate the principle of unrestricted reciprocity ; but that was quite consistent with their advocacy at the same time of a revenue tariff; and I believe it is the uniform opinion in Canada to-day-and in this I believe hon. members opposite agree with me-that a very large measure of reciprocity between Canada and the United States in matters of trade is a most desirable thing, in the interests of both countries. But throughout, the policy of a revenue tariff continued. Then, Sir, in order that there might be no question at all about what their policy was, the Liberals of Canada from one end of the country to the other met in Ottawa in the year 1893 and solemnly laid down their policy in black and white, and spread it broadcast throughout the country, making- it so plain that all men could understand it; and in that declaration they said they would have a tariff for the purposes of revenue. Did they not carry out that pledge within a few months after they came into office ?
All these facts are just as well known by hon. gentlemen opposite as by hon. members on this side of the House. If that be so, why is there this persistent misrepresentation of the Liberal position on the question of the tariff ? I could point out without any very great difficulty some Conservative inconsistencies with regard to the same matter. I can certainly point out inconsistencies in the Conservative view of the Liberal tariff. Why, Sir, when the hon. Finance Minister introduced his tariff in the spring of 1897, hon. members opposite almost to a man stood up and denounced it. They said, you have produced a ruinous-

tariff, the attack being led by the hon. gentleman who then led the opposition. He said : You will bring ruin to every industry of Canada if you maintain a tariff of that kind. That was their first position. But when they saw that the industries of the country were going to prosper under the new tariff, that there was going to be no stagnation, but advance and improvement, they changed their song, and said : You have stolen our clothes ; you are maintaining the old policy of protection.
Now, Sir, is it not a reasonable thing to ask that the present tariff and the policy of this government upon the question of ' the tariff should be judged by its fruits ? I submit that if you judge it merely as an academic problem, or by the results which it has produced in this country, you must come to the same conclusion, that the government are justified in maintaining it. 1 do not go so far as to say that the tariff is complete, that it is entirely without error. I know some details myself which in my judgment ought to be corrected. But, Sir, it would be a wrong thing at such a time, when trade has become established on certain lines, for any government to interfere with the details of a tariff which would cause unrest throughout the business community. One thing that the present tariff has given to the country, which it never enjoyed before, is stability in the duties levied upon the various articles.
The hon. leader of the opposition said, how can you argue that you have a revenue tariff when you have a surplus? and to back up his theory that a revenue tariff and a surplus are inconsistent, he quoted some utterances of the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) away back in 1882, and read some newspaper articles of 1882 which he attributed to the hon. Minister of Finance.
To my mind there is absolutely no inconsistency at all in having a surplus with a revenue tariff. The hon. gentleman knows precisely how a surplus comes about. He knows that the revenue of the country is estimated before it is collected. He knows that the Finance Minister makes a careful estimate of his expenditure and his revenue, and there can be little doubt that if the Finance Minister wished, he could so adjust his tariff that there would not be much of a surplus. I do not think he could come exactly within the figures, but he could come relatively nearer to the exact amount required than he has come this year. But why not have a surplus? Why not be on the safe side in your finances ? If all the money that was required in this country were merely the common annual expenditure of the country, then it would be a wrong thing to have a surplus under a revenue tariff. But we require far more money than we get. Far more money is spent in Canada
than is represented by the annual expenditure. Take this year for example: The hon. Finance Minister says he expects to spend about $46,400,000; that is the ordinary annual expenditure. In addition to that, he expects to spend about $10,500,000 on permanent public works and improvements. That brings the expenditure up to about $57,000,000 ; yet all he expects to receive during the year is $53,000,000 He could have pruned his duties to have brought his revenue down to the $46,400,000 if he had so desired. Then he would either have had to abandon the public improvements or he would have had to go and borrow the whole amount necessary to make them. Which course is he to pursue ? The course the government adopts is : We will permit the accumulation of a reasonable amount of revenue, and when it accumulates we will spend it on the public works of the country. We will carry on these public works, and if the surplus is not sufficient to pay the cost, then the small balance will be the amount by which our debt will be increased. I submit that that is good financing. I submit that it is right to provide a small surplus annually, in order that we may expend it in this way. Far better that we should do that than borrow the whole amount we may require and pay interest. That, at all events, is the plan which the Minister of Finance has adopted, and there is nothing whatever in that plan inconsistent with the maintenance of a revenue tariff.
I have also heard it charged that ours is not a revenue tariff, beceause we grant bounties, and bounties are the most extreme form of protection. Well, Mr. Speaker, the bounty system, I admit, is a protective system, and admit also that I am not opposed to the bounty system so long as it is kept within reasonable bounds That, I think, is the principle on which the present government is working. Here, for instance, is a particular industry which needs assistance, and is going to become a permanent improvement and of great value in the development of the country, and to this industry the government agree to pay a bounty. No doubt, that is a principle of protection, and I am so far a protectionist that I agree with that prinicple so long as [DOT] it is kept within reasonable bounds. I was glad to hear the Minister of Finance declare, iu reply to the hon. member for West York (Mr. Wallace), that the subject of lead bounties was under discussion. Personally. I see no objection to a reasonable amount being expended in the development of the lead industry, just as such an amount is being expended in the development of the iron industry.
But, what objection is there, on the other hand, to charging these bounties against capital account ? One of the charges made by the hon. member for West York was.

that we were charging these bounties against capital account and not against annual expenditure. Is not that the proper way ? Are these bounties an annual expenditure V Are they not precisely in the same position as railway subsidies ? Does not parliament vote railway subsidies solely on the principle that they are going to develop the country and will be permanent improvements ? If parliament does not vote them on that principle, parliament should not vote them at all. They are voted on the ground that they are going to develop the country, and are in the nature of permanent Improvements. Where is that money charged ? It is charged to capital account. Where did the hon. member for West York charge such subsidies when in power 7 He charged them to capital account. Where did every government that was ever in power in this country charge railway subsidies they charged them to capital account. Then, why not charge bounties to the same account. They are not in the nature of expenditure going on from year to year, but will only go on for a few years and then cease. They go to improve the country in a permanent way and should be charged to capital account and not to annual expenditure.
These are matters whicn struck me during the course of this discussion, but there is one other to which I wish to refer before leaving the subject. I think it was the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Kemp) who said that the policy of the government was driving people out of the country, and that men were actually leaving Canada for want of employment. Is not that entirely contrary to the facts ? Is it not within the knowledge of every hon. member here that men have come back in large numbers from the United States during the past four years ? Is it not a fact that there has been such great mercantile and commercial and industrial development in this country that more labour was necessary than has been employed, and a great portion of the additional labour consists of Canadians, who were expatriated a few years ago but have now returned to Canada ? In proof of that statement, take the wail of the New England millowners, that they cannot get operatives for their mills. And' what reason do they give? They say that so many French Canadian operatives have gone back to Canada that the mills are short of hands. Take the farms of Michigan, which have been abandoned, and the lumber mills, which cannot get hands, and what reason is given for this lack of labour ? It is that the men have gone back to Canada. Is it not within the knowledge of every hon. member, in the particular locality in which he may happen to reside, that many men have come back to reside in their own town who had gone from Canada to the United States in the last ten or fifteen years?
As between Canada and the United States,
the movement of population has been entirely in favour of this country. It has caused serious talk on the other side of the line, not only on the question of population, but also on the question of the export of our food products to the old country.
I will not occupy your time further, but will merely advert to the remaining sections of the amendment, and shall do so very briefly indeed. If there is one thing for which I admire the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Ivemp) it is his courage and persistence in carrying on the debate on that question of preferential trade within the empire, after the manner in which the fallacy of that clause of the amendment had been exposed during the past forty-eight hours in this House. We admire courage and persistence, but I noticed that it was all courage, and nothing to back it up in the shape of reason, because I failed to recognize a single new fact which the hon. member brought to the attention of the House while he endeavoured to convince us that we should give our support to the second clause of that amendment.
Are hon. members opposite sincere in their desire to have Imperial or preferential trade between Canada and Great Britain, as is proposed by the amendment ? If they are sincere in that view, they snould stop their denunciations of the one act of the Canadian parliament which has brought that greater question within the range of possibility. I refer to the preference which we now give to the goods of the mother land. I have heard it stated here, time and time again, during the course of this debate, that the preference we give Great Britain is no preference at all, that our imports from Great Britain have not increased, that our exports have increased, but not to a greater extent than those to the United States. That may be true, but there is reason for it. The recent increase in exports of the United States to Great Britain is not in connection with goods which Canada produces, but in connection with goods which the United States export and Canada does not. It is in connection with the production of iron and steel probably that the greatest increase is noticeable. But that is an infant industry in Canada, which is rapidly rising to be a great industry. But where we have disturbed our competitors and where the benefit of the preference is noticeable in Canada, is with regard to the agricultural or finished food products which we are exporting to Great Britain. In the matter of cheese, bacon, butter and the like. Canada has far outstripped the United States since the preference was inaugurated, and nobody recognizes that fact more plainly than our friends to the south.
I heard the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) express the most earnest solicitude on behalf of the Canadian farmer.

I was surprised to hear the hon. member tor West Toronto do so. He seemed to think that the government of Canada had committed a grievous wrong on the Canadian farmer, because, one result of our preference to Great Britan was a discriminating tariff against Canada on the part of Germany. That may be one of the results. But did not the hon. member for West Toronto realize what a relatively small quantity of goods from this country seeks German markets and what a tremendously large quantity finds its way to British markets? Does he think the Canadian farmer is mourning over the condition of affairs now so vastly improved over what it was a few years ago ? Why, if he had expressed his solicitude for these poor farmers, as he put it, five or six years ago, I have no doubt the farmers would have appreciated his sympathy. He has not a single farmer in his constituency, I am persuaded. But he did honour the constituency which I have the honour to represent by sending up some seed grain prior to the last election. That, at all events, is my information on the subject.
Now, is there anything more manifest than this-that the farmers of Canada are in a much better position than they have been in any time in the last fifteen years ? Is there any better satisfied portion of this community than the agricultural population ? I can tell the hon. member for West Toronto that if the appeal of the government in November last had been solely upon its financial policy and only to the farmers of the country, the result would have been that the ruin which has been wrought in the ranks of our opponents would be as nothing to the ruin which would have followed an appeal limited to the farmers of Canada. The farmers are prosperous, the farmers are satisfied. They do not want parliament or the government to interfere with that preferential arrangement in favour of the goods of the mother land ifor the sake of a few paltry hundreds or thousands of dollars thalt might have found their way into the German market on even terms with the rest of the world. I prefer to leave that question of German discrimination as the Prime Minister left it. 1 think that the mode suggested by the Prime Minister to the leader of the opposition was accepted by that hon. gentleman as the proper one for dealing with this question. It should not be brought up here for discussion ; we should not get into heated debate over it, until the government has exhausted all its powers of bringing about a satisfactory arrangement with the German Empire. Until that time, I think, our discussion is out of place. But this reference to the German tariff is not more out of place in this discussion than other clauses of the amendment are out of place. Is there any reason why there should be a change in the fiscal policy of the country ? It is true there are
some manufacturers that would like better terms. The hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Kemp) felt very sore that any one should mention that the manufacturers had been coming to Ottawa to ask that changes should be made in the tariff. But it is a fact that they have been coming-numerous deputations have come. Manufacturers are only human beings and, like other men. they want to get all the assistance and all the preference they can. And if their coming to Ottawa has the result of securing for them special terms, they will continue to come, but they must not complain if some of their requests cannot be granted. Such sensible business men as the hon. member for East Toronto should not take offence at a mere reference to the class of which he is an honoured member. There is nothing in the affairs of this country, financial, commercial, or otherwise to justify any change an our fiscal policy ; but, on the other hand, I submit that if you will judge this tariff, the revenue tariff of the present administration by the results that have been brought about, one and all will say that the government is perfectly justified in maintaining that tariff.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that on this side of the House no fault will be found with the remarks made by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie). I certainly think both sides will thank him very cordially for the lecture he has read the House on the proper method of conducting debate. He started out by telling us that there should be a higher standard of debate in this House, and in a rather eloquent burst he portrayed the greatness of English parliaments in the past in which there had been Cobdens and Brights. I presume his modesty forbade him, in the presence of the ministers, instituting a comparison between those hon. gentlemen and the giants of the English Liberalism of the past. But he did make a striking reflection upon the ministers who were present and listening to him. when he held up Bright and Cobden as men who were always martyrs to principle. Certainly he could not lay i,t at the doors of these ministers that they had ever been true to any principle. Principles they may have known, buit principles as things to be suffered for were put behind them long ago. Nature has been kind to them. They are like the famous American politician who said :
A merciful Providence fashioned us holler,
In order that we might our principles swaller.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Guthrie) early in his speech spoke in this high and lofty strain, and I would have thought that, coming from the constituency he does come from-South Wellington, a very grand constituency-he would have represented these high principles of propriety and of elevated

public life there as lie does here. But I notice that the other clay a banquet was- very worthily no doubt-tendered to him, and he did not condescend to tell the people there of the high state of morality which should exist in politics and the high standard to be maintained; but he did ted the people that they were led up as sheep to the shambles. He explained that the reason why the constituency did not go Liberal in 1896, was because the Liberals had carried on a campaign of cash and wind
1 hope the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) will excuse me for in-terupting him, but I desire to say that I used no such expression.
I will read from the Toronto Globe
I have read that report- it is wrong.

The hon. gentleman spoke somewhat late in the evening and no doubt this banquet having been in the town of Guelph was not a cold water affair. He is reported as saying that in 1896 the Liberals of South Wellington had fought a campaign of wind and cash, but that his campaign had been one of hard work and hence success. If he was reported correctly, he paid a poor tribute indeed to the intelligence of his constituency in intimating that it was up for bargain and sale. In his speech of this evening the hon. gentleman went on to discuss the policy of the present administration-if policy it may be called. In one thing the hon. gentleman is to be congratulated. He has no unhappy past to look back upon. He is not like the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) or the hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding)-he has nothing to apologize for, because he has not been committed to any principle. He has taken his stand, and, I think fairly well. He is a protectionist as long as the protectionist policy is favourable, but the moment it becomes otherwise he is willing, like the ministers, to set his sails to any varying wind. I propose to deal for a little time with some remarks he made with reference to some questions of the debate. He commenced by commenting on the amendment which has been moved by the leader of the opposition. He said he wished to know from this side of the House where this party stood. Well, if the hon. gentleman will take pains to read the resolution he will find where this party stands. He asks if this party is prepared to increase the protective duties on any particular articles; if they are, he says, here is the time and place to do it. Now, let us see what the resolution says :
That, in the opinion of this House, the welfare of the country requires a pronounced policy of adequate protection and encouragement at all Mr. BENNETT.
times to the labour, agricultural, manufacturing, mining and other Industrial interests of Canada.
Surely there is no uncertain sound about that. It says the country requires a pronounced policy. From this side of the House no apology need go forth as to the past of this party. For over twenty-five years it has stood for a policy of pronounced protection. But here is this marked difference between us and hon. gentlemen opposite, that while we have to a great extent adopted and fallen in line with a protective policy, they have at all times intimated, and by insinuation threatened, that at the earliest possible moment this policy will be cut in twain, or shorn of much of its strength. But it is to be noticed that these hon. gentlemen always have an attachment in the shape of some friendly manufacturers of the same political faith, and the result is that these gentlemen remain protectionists in certain lines and relative to certain industries. Now, there can be no more marked line of conduct mapped out than there is in that resolution stating that the policy of protection must be a pronounced policy. And now we have the warning note that has been sounded by the Minister of Finance, when he told the people of this country, and more particularly the manufacturers, that the time has arrived when they must take in sail, that a commercial storm is coming on. That is a declaration not only to the manufacturers of this country, but to the labouring classes and the agricultural interests as well, and indeed to every interest, because every interest is dependent on the manufacturing interests of the country. I say in view of all these facts it is time for the country to see where the present government stands. If this government is honest in what it says, why have they not the courage to take the tariff as it stands to-day ? The First Minister said yesterday in the House that there was a certain amount of protection on many items, and to his mind that protection should be lessened and reduced. The Minister of the Interior speaking the other day made this remark :
When we give a preference if it is to be at any one's expense, it is at the expense of the manufacturer and workingmen of Canada. We go a little further and say that it is the policy of the Liberal party of Canada to reduce the duties and to remove to some extent the burdens of the excessive tariff which was imposed upon imported goods by the late Conservative government.
He shows that there are dozens of cases where goods are coming in from the United States, and from that country alone, where the duties are to-day exactly what they were under Conservative rule. Then in the name of all that is honest when these gentlemen denounce that protection, why have they not the honesty to attack
it and reduce the duties ? But they do not rest there. The Minister of Finance, speaking in the House a couple of years ago-I think it was on the occasion of the announcement of the preference-said that the manufacturers of this country must take notice from this time forward thalt they were not promised immunity from cuts in the tariff, that this might take place on any occasion, and that they should take heed. As I already remarked, the First Minister yesterday made the statement that there was already tariff protection beyond what there should be. I say, then, in face of these statements of these hon. gentlemen, it is time for us and for the country to understand where both parties stand. The amendment moved by the hon. gentleman who leads the opposition states clearly and explicitly that we are going to adhere to a pronounced policy of adequate protection, and there is not going to be on this side of the House from one quarter and from one section a defence of protection, and from another quarter hon. gentlemen standing up in their places and denouncing that policy, as they are doing on the government side to-day, and from different ministers of the Crown we hear these statements and insinuations that they believe that that policy should be cut in two. But, Sir, it is in keeping with the profession of hon. gentlemen ; they think one thing and they do directly the opposite.
Now, Sir, the hon. gentleman then dealt with the question of a tariff for revenue only, and he went over the old song that this was only a tariff for revenue. Why, Sir, fancy a city council or a town council yearly striking their rate, and at the end of the year having a surplus of $8,000 or $10,000. Would it be said that they had simply struck a rate for revenue and for revenue alone ? The fact of the matter is that these gentlemen are so held up by certain political friends of their own that they are bound in obedience to the wishes of those friends to maintain a high protective tariff on many goods coming into this country from the United States, and that is the reason for the high revenue that has been produced. There are other reasons no doubt for that revenue, one has been the increased values ; and no doubt falling values in this country is one reason why the Minister of Finance saw fit to sound the warning that he did the other day. Another point the hon. gentleman dealt with at considerable length was this: That the time had arrived in this country, in view of affairs as they stand, that we should endeavour to negotiate with the United States a reciprocity treaty. Well, I can only say that the hon. gentleman cannot have read the debates, and particularly the speech of his leader in this House, I think a year or two ago, when he made the statement that the time had gone past
in this country for any reciprocity with the United States, that our markets was the market of Great Britain, and not the market of the United States alone. That is a difference between the hon. gentleman and his leader which they will have to reconcile between themselves.
But the hon. gentleman was happy in one thing : He laid down as his political belief and entire honesty of opinion that he was in favour of iron bounties. He was not like the Minister of Trade and Commerce, hampered with a past ; he had not stood up in the House and on public platforms year after year and denounced the policy of giving iron bounties. But the hon. gentleman goes further to-night and says that he is not content to give a bounty on iron only, but he proposes to give bounties on lead as well. That is another point in respect of which the hon. gentleman is to be congratulated on the fact that he has not a political past.
Now, Sir, the hon. gentleman said that we should endeavour to restrict ourselves to questions of trade and commerce, leaving out what might be termed extraneous matters, and I propose briefly to discuss some matters in that line. The First Minister yesterday drew a line between our policy as enunciated by our leader, and the policy of the government, in the course of which he made this striking statement.
We agree with them that the revenue of the country ought to be levied by means of customs duties; but there is this difference between us, that while they would levy those duties only for the benefit of individuals, we levy them for the benefit of the revenue, first and foremost.
Now, if customs duties are only levied for the purpose of raising sufficient money to carry on the affairs of the country, then in the name of reason why do they tax people $8,000,000 more than is necessary for that purpose ? He went on to say :
Our first consideration, in imposing duties, is to produce revenue, and if, as an incident, the manufacturers derive advantage, they are welcome to it. But gentlemen on the other side impose duties, not with a view of levying a revenue and putting money into the treasury, but of putting money into the pockets of private individuals.
Now, let us take the tariff as it stands to-day, and more particularly in reference to the articles which are imported from the United States, hardly a dollar's worth of which comes in from Great Britain, and consequently do not get the benefit of the preference. What does the Minister of Trade and Commerce say 'to his leader's proposition ? He almost admitted that the duty on furniture is the same as it was prior to these hon. gentlemen coming into power ; and will the Minister of Customs contend to-night that the duty on furniture is levied for the purposes of producing a revenue ? If it is levied simply for the purpose of

protection and not for revenue, why do hon. gentlemen not cut down the duties on furniture, let us have less revenue from that source, and let us have the benefit of the lessened price ? Take the question of carriages ; if there was any one part of the population to which these hon. gentlemen, when in opposition, did appeal, it was to the farmers of the country. How the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce and the hon. Minister of Customs used to cry over the woes of the farmers ! The duty on coal oil was an abomination to them. If the hon. gentlemen only came to power there would be a revolution in trade matters, and the way in which the hon. Minister of Customs, who is present to-night, and the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce, hope to relieve the farmer is by increasing the duty on the cutter that he is bringing in from the United States. Was that to raise the revenue ? If taxing the farmer's cutter was for the purpose of raising the revenue, why did not the hon. Minister of Customs tax the jewellery of the rich in order to produce revenue ? The hon. Minister of Customs may follow in this debate, and it will certainly be amusing to hear the hon. gentleman try to reconcile himself to the position, that when he wants to raise the revenue, he does not increase the duty on the jewellery of the rich but increases the duty on the farmers' cutters. These hon. gentlemen wanted to increase the revenue, and as a result they have taxed the tobacco of the poor man, they have taxed the sugar of the poor and the rice of the poor, raising upwards of $2,000,000 of revenue by the increase on those articles. They are taxing the boots and shoes and some other articles which are not imported at all from Great Britain, upon which no preference is obtainable, but which come in from the United States, and these hon. gentlemen are not at all imposing these duties simply for the purpose of raising a revenue, but they are giving what they have to give, and what I am glad they have to give- protection to the manufacturing industries of the country. Ilad these hon. gentlemen been true to their pledges prior to 1890. they would have been swept out of Ontario and out of the whole Dominion on the 7th of November. The hon. member for South Wellington spoke of these hon. gentlemen having principles. We have found that their only principle is the principle of distributing amongst themselves loaves and fishes and hanging on to their salaries. If there was one question above all others that these hon. gentlemen have waxed eloquent over, it was the question of the duty on coal and iron. One could turn up in the newspapers of the time speech after speech delivered by the hon. Minister of Customs himself, in which he pointed out to the farmers that their agricultural implements were too high in price because of the duty on coal and iron. He said that Mr. BENNETT.
high bounties were paid to the producers of iron, and for that reason agricultural implements were too dear. He said that if these men could not maintain themselves without these bounties and high duties, let them go to the wall. Now, the hon. Minister of Customs knows that he made that statement time and time again ; he knows that he waxed eloquent over it. The hon. gentleman sits there now, smiles benignly, and draws his salary, while he is false to his principles. There is another feature of this question, and it is that if these hou. gentlemen were afraid that by lessening the duties they would diminish the revenue, there was a good way for them to get out of the difficulty, and that was by making good the pledges of economy which they gave to the people. Why, they made the welkin ring from one end of the Dominion to the other. In regard to the number of cabinet ministers, they pointed to the example of the United States, where there is a less number of ministers, and they said : When we come into power there is going to be a lesser number of ministers, and all along the line lai'ge economies are to be practised. The hon. Minister of Customs knows how well that pledge was kept. As soon as the government achieved power, he was advanced from the position of a controller to that of a minister, and they paid him a year and a half of back salary, or, as an hon. gentleman says, two years salary. These gentlemen, who are compared with Cobden and Bright, with men who were willing to go out of office at any time by reason of adherence to their principles, have nothing in common with such statesmen. There is nothing in common between the two ; all their principles have vanished and gone to the winds. The hon. member touched upon the question of the British preference, but he touched that rather gingerly, and very little was said in reference to it. As the question is an important one to the people of the country, 1 intend to take up the time of the House for a few moments in regard to it. Where do the political parties stand on the question of the British preference ? The right hon. leader of the government was yesterday assailed by the hon. leader of the opposition in this, that he went before the electors, and, notably in his speech in Dondon. committed himself to the policy of preferential trade with Great Britain. What can be meant by preferential trade if not a mutual preference conceded on either side ? These hon. gentlemen, realizing that this policy was a popular one, adopted it in the elections prior to 1890. went to the country, and told the people they were favourable to a preferential duty. We all know that at that time there was a strong feeling being worked up in England in that direction. Mr. Chamberlain's utterances on different occasions pointed to that fact, and when the movement was blooming, it
was all swept away upon the occasion of the fateful trip of the right hon. leader of the government to England, when he declared in London, at the celebrated meeting of the Cobden Glub, that Canada did not want a preference at all. So, these hon. gentlemen are in this position that they are averse to having a preference for Canadian products in the markets of Great Britain, while we stand committed by the text of this resolution to the principle of a mutual preference between this country and Great Britain, and by that policy we are prepared to stand. In the same connection, I would refer to the question of trade with Germany, and I beg to state that we are here to-night to say, and the Conservative party are a unit on that, I believe, and not only the party here, but, I believe, a very large number of Liberals throughout the country, are in accord with the sentiment, that any country, Germany, or whatever it. may be, which pronounces against us by an antagonistic tariff, will be met by us, that we are not going to lie under such a rebuke, but that we are going to hit back, and hit back with double force. That proposition should be doubly favourable in me dominion of Canada, by reason of the fact that everybody knows that under this so-called British tariff, which is a sham and a delusion, there is no counti'y which is getting greater benefits in Canada than Germany itself. What is the position of hon. gentlemen opposite on this question 7 When they first came here with that policy they made the statement that the policy would work out all right, that Canada would only import British goods ; but it was pointed out that the British market was being invaded by German, Belgian and other European goods, and that we would of necessity be importing these goods under the British preference tariff. It was then stated that a considerable portion of the work on these goods must of necessity be done in Great Britain before they would be entitled to the preference. It was easy to, tell the House that, but a difference arose in the minds of the appraisers of customs at different ports of Canada as to what really was a considerable portion of the work, and the result was that hon. gentlemen were forced to announce a new proposition, and that was, that so long as 25 per cent of the work upon these articles was done in Great Britain, they would get the benefit of the preference. To-day, as a matter of fact, the preference is not upon 25 per cent in favour of Great Britain, but upon 75 per cent in favour of Germany. While Germany is prepared to strike at us, I say it behooves the people of Canada to strike back, and, speaking for myself, I say that I believe that the interests of the artisans and the manufacturers of Canada should stand higher with any governemnt of Canada than the interests of Great Britain or any other country. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Guthrie) made
some very wild statements as to the beneficial effect on Canada of sentiment in Great Britain. He told us that our exports to Great Britain had gone up by leaps and bounds by reason of this preferential tariff, but if he had taken the trouble to consult the statistics he would know that the reverse is the case. He told us that we exported more cheese to Great Britain than we did a few years ago, but in that he was mistaken. He does not seem to know anything about it. Here are the actual figures on that score. In 1898 we exported to Great Britain 196,220,771 pounds of cheese, and last year we exported 185,759,750 pounds, a decrease in round numbers of 11,000,000 pounds. Where does the question of sentiment come in there ? In 1898 we exported 8,429,249 pounds of ham, and last year we exported only 2,793,078 pounds. We do not seem to have sold more hams because of the sympathy in Great Britain for our preferential tariff. I might go on and quote further to show that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Guthrie) was far astray when he talked of sentiment increasing the trade between Canada and Great Britain. Why, the fact is, and every common-sense business man knows it, that the Britisher will buy the necessaries for himself and his family in the cheapest market, and he will not pay half a farthing a pound more for sentiment. I contend, Sir, that the preference to Great Britain is not in the interests of the people of this country as a whole. Experience proves that we import from Great Britain such commodities as are not used by the masses of the people, but rather by the classes, and therefore whatever benefit there is in the preference is a benefit to the more wealthy of the people of this country. Look at the Trade and Navigation Returns to prove that. In 1898 of silk and manufactures of silk we imported $1,413,973 worth, whilst last year we imported $3,151,697 worth. There is a marked increase in an article that is used by the wealthy classes of this country, and as a result the rich instead of the poor are getting the benefit of this preference. Take the importation of jewellery. In 1896 we imported $295,141 worth, and in 1899 we imported $578,785 worth. If you go through the returns it will be shown that . the articles which are imported from Great Britain to a great extent are not used by the masses, but by the wealthy classes. The Minister of Finance in his budget speech announced that the time had arrived when the people of Canada should take heed as to the future. Any one who looks around the country and sees the existing conditions will know at a glance there can be no doubt as to that. In the town of Almonte a large woollen mill has been closed down. There are other woollen industries in the province of Ontario closed down to-day, and you cannot go into any

town in the province, more particularly in towns where there are manufacturing enterprises, that you do not see signs of depression. In the once thriving town of Paris in South Brant there is advertised a house for sale with a recommendation that it would be a desirable summer resort. Has it come to pass that the once manufacturing town of Paris is reduced to a summer resort ? In South Ontario, the once thriving town of Whitby, where the Joseph Hall agricultural implement works were, has a place advertised as a desirable summer residence for people living in Toronto. All over, the fact stares you in the face that the time has arrived when we have got to do what the United States are doing, namely, make for ourselves a protective tariff and by that protective tariff stand or fall.
Hear, hear.

There can be no doubt in the public mind as to where the two political parties stand on this question. The Conservative party stands where It always did stand, and that is : That so long as the great people of the United States are manufacturing as they are, there is only one recourse for the people of Canada, and that is to maintain a high protective tariff. Now, Sir, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Guthrie) made the statement that had there only been the question of the policy of the government brought into the last elections in Ontario, the government would have made a better showing. He did not assign any reason why the gov-erenment did not have a larger following from Ontario, but he must know very well why the Liberal saddles were emptied in that province. Year in and year out for eighteen years the Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson), the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) .and others of their ilk, proclaimed for commercial union at one time, for free trade at another time, for unrestricted reciprocity with the United States at another time, but they were always the undying foes of protection in every shape and form. They pictured to the farmers that they were being bled white for the benefit of the manufacturers, and that they were bearing the heat and burden of the day, while the manufacturers were growing rich. The farmers took them at their word. They believed they were honest men.
Oh.

The farmers listened to them for years and believed them, but when the opportunity came these gentlemen deceived the farmers. The Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson) knew the storm was coming. He saw the last Speaker of this House (Mr. Bain) quit politics because he had not the hardihood

to go into his riding after his party friends had violated ail their pledges, and that riding is represented to-day by a Conservative. Where is the former member for North Wellington (Mr. "McMullen), who posed throughout all Canada as the apostle of economy. He too has been buried with the Liberal dead. I could go along those benches opposite and name the member from Ontario who year after year denounced extravagance and iniquity when in opposition, but who, when in power, practiced what they denounced. And where are they to-day ? Well, some of them who for years in this House denounced the Senate as charnel house for dead and decayed politicians, have been fortunate enough to secure a resting place in the Upper Chamber ; others have got comfortable positions in the government service, and the balance are trying to get there. The government met us in the fight and they defeated us.
But there is no man knows better in his heart than the premier himself that this government has got the greatest slap that any government ever got in the province of Ontario. The reason they got that slap was that the people of Ontario were prepared to take these hon. gentlemen at their word, and they were weighed in the balances, and were found wanting. The hon. member for London (Mr. Hyman) the other night said: ' If we have lost in Ontario, remember we have captured Quebec.' The hon. gentlemen are quite welcome to have Quebec on the terms they- got it. They conducted a campaign of race and religion in the province of Quebec ; and wherever they could introduce the same campaign in the province of Ontario, they did so, and did so successfully. They introduced it in Glengarry, which has a large French population, and that is the reason they carried that county. They introduced it in the two ridings of Essex, where there is also a large French population, and that is the reason they carried them. I was amused at hearing the hon. member for Bona-venture (Mr. Marcil), in seconding the address this session, express the hope that these cries of race and religion would be buried and put out of sight. That hon. gentleman was in my riding in 1897, when there was a by-election. I had been unseated. At that time the French Canadians-and there are about 500 voters in that locality-were sympathizing very keenly with their fellow-countrymen in Manitoba, who they thought were deprived of their school rights. The hon. member for Bonaventure came there. He did not appear in the English parts of the constituency, but he could be found in the French settlements day in and day out. And the hon. gentleman never came back to redeem the pledge which he made on that occasion. The pledge was this : He first asked that
the government might he excused for not having passed a Remedial Bill in their first session, on the ground that they had not time ; but he said there was a session coming on in 1897, and if a Remedial Bill were not passed then, he would come hack there and denounce the government at the earliest opportunity. The hon. member has not been there since. He will be like all the Liberal speakers who come into that part of the riding, firing the heather, as they do, with incendiary speeches on race and religion. I do not presume that he will ever come back. If he does, he will be the first of the kind who ever did. They always come with the same old story. Wherever they find a French Canadian population in Ontario, they are found making these incendiary speeches.
The hon. gentlemen have brought this fight on themselves. They have done it all through the province of Quebec, and I believe that as the people of Quebec rejected the Mercier government for pillaging the country, in the same way they will reject this government. These hon. gentlemen have won, but how have they won ? They have won by setting province against province. They have lost in the province of Ontario ; they have won in the province of Quebec. True, they have gained some advantages in some of the other provinces; but from the banner province of Ontario they have come back disorganized, broken up and battered in a way that no political party ever came from that province before. And when these hon. gentlemen again pass in review before the people of this country, then we shall be prepared to leave the issue to the people ; and the great issue that must divide the two parties in the next general election, so far as we on this side of the House are concerned, must be that Canada shall have, if it is in the power of a Liberal-Conservative government to grant it, that measure of protection to the artisans, the merchants, the manufacturers and the agriculturists, which will make Canada the happy and contented country that it has been under the benign influence of the national policy which was introduced by the Liberal-Conservative party in 1879.

Mr. Speaker, I do not suppose I should add much to the dignity of this discussion, if I were to follow the example which has just been set by my hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) who has just taken his seat. The strength of the blow which the government received in Ontario, or the manner of their victory in Quebec, or anything appertaining to the elections which recently took place, are matters very far removed from the subject of the debate. I am not aware that the fact that there is a summer residence to let in the town of Paris has much to do with the great question now engaging our attention. But I take exception to one statement which the hon. gentleman made, that the British preference was of no use to the people of this country. If it has been of no other use than to reduce the burden of taxation by 25 per cent on all British goods, that in itself would be a justification for the introduction of the preferential tariff. It not only brought about that reduction, but it also reduced the cost price of all goods with which imported British goods come into competition. But I do not desire to enter into that phase of the discussion. I wish to confine myself to the question before the House. I am quite willing to leave the foraging around amongst elections and the history of Canada since confederation to our friends opposite, and try to deal with subjects which are germane to the conditions by which we are surrounded.
I desire, before I address myself to the resolution, to find a little fault with some remarks that fell from the leader of the opposition-not because they were grave in themselves, but because they assume a gravity coming from one who occupies the position he does as one of the leaders in this House. He stated-and he appeared to reproach us for it-that our trade with the United States was assuming larger proportions every day. Now, I do not think there is any reason why he should feel sorrowful because our trade with the United States is growing larger every day. A trade that is growing larger, no matter with whom it is being conducted, results to the benefit of those who engage in it, or they would not continue it for a single day. Our people do not import largely from the United States because they especially like goods from the United States. We buy there, because we can buy there cheaper than we can anywhere else in the world, and cheaper than we can produce the goods for ourselves. The fact that we imported from the United States last year a hundred million dollars worth of goods is not a matter of regret to me, but one of great satisfaction, which would be only enhanced were the amount two hundred million of dollars instead of one hundred million. No trade can be carried on between nations that is not mutually profitable ; and the mere fact that the trade exists between the United States and ourselves is the best evidence that it is profitable, or it would not be continued. I go still further, and say that if we bought from the United States large quantities of goods and they did not buy a single cent's worth from us, there would be no evidence that that trade was not profitable to us ; because it does not matter with whom we do trade, it is always bound to be profitable. Let us take the two items of coal and corn. The United States is the only country in the world where we can buy coal and corn as cheaply as we buy



There is not an English statesman that has given any greater encouragement than that: We may give you free trade, but that is the only basis on which we can even discuss tne matter. Are we prepared to discuss the mutual preference on the basis of free trade? Is there a man on either side of this House who would accept a mutual preference of that kind And is there the faintest possibility of Canada getting a preference of any other kind than one based upon the principles of free trade '! I challenge any lion, gentleman on either side of the House to mention the name of a British statesman who has ever given them the slightest encouragement to believe that they could get it on any other terms. The only man who has said that it was capable of being discussed even on the basis of free trade is Mr. Chamberlain himself. Lord Rosebery is against it. Sir -uiehael Hicks-Beach. the Chancellor of the Exchequer is against it, the president of the board of trade is against it. All the great leaders of public opinion have spoken against this preferential policy; they have said that it would ruin the empire, instead of making it stronger ; they have said it would be a standing menace to the nations of the world and would array against Great Britain and her colonies the powers of the world in a commercially hostile attitude. I can quote the words of Lord Rosebery and of Sir Michael Hicks-Beach and Mr. Ritchie, the president of the board of trade. And 1 will quote his words in order to set my hon. friend from East Toronto (Mr. Kemp) straight. To-day. I asked that lion, gentleman to read all of the address from Mr. D. Ritchie. He did not have it handy apparently or he did not want to read it. I will read it now, in order that the House may understand exactly what Mr. Ritchie did say :
He thought that the strict Manchester school was passing away, and although England would never depart from her free trade policy, she might arrange a closer connection with Greater Britain. How this was to be done he did not indicate.
That is what the hon. gentleman said on that occasion, and what was read to-day. But he said more than that. His language was considered by some who were present to have given encouragement to the idea that a preference would be given to some of the colonies; and, later on, at the same meeting he craved the indulgence of the audience to disabuse their minds of any such idea :
Mr. Ritchie subsequently asked leave to say that he in no way favoured the imposition of duties on any manufactured article imported into this country. It seemed to him impossible to conceive that a 5 per cent duty on our foreign imports would help the colonies, and he strongly supported the fundamental principles of free trade. So that his remarks about a possible plan for a zollverein was. a mere pious wish.

That is a portion of Mr. Ritchie's speech that the hon. member for East Toronto did not read, and the impression that he tried to convey to this House that the president of the British Board of Trade was in favour of this, was misleading, because be did not give us that gentleman's opinion, who says himself that he is opposed to Interfering with the principles of free trade. Vv nat does Lord Rosebery say ?
Of all the mad things we have heard in our days, the re-enactment of the corn laws is the
maddest we can possibly conceive.
What does Mr. Chamberlain say V
But the principle which I claim must be accepted if we are to make any, even the slightest, progress is that within the different parts of the empire protection must disappear.
What does Mr. Mulkall say, the great statistician who has just passed away ?
Mutual trade preference in favour of the colonies of the empire would be ruinous to the latter, and would ultimately break up the empire.
We have here the testimony of the men of Great Britain who speak with authority, and who state that they cannot discuss the proposition except on the basis of free trade. We have the authority of such men as Rosebery, Mulhall and others that it would be ruinous to the empire. Yet in face of these strong declarations of these men who speak with authority, whose position in the political world of Great Britain gives significance to whut they say, our friends opposite deliberately introduce a resolution which they know is entirely impracticable, because it would be injurious to the people of Canada. They know that we can get no preference in Great Britain on any principle but that of free trade. Are they prepared to accept that ? Not one of them has the courage to say that they value a preference in Great Britain high enough to he willing to destroy the manufacturing interests of this country.
1 am quite willing to accept any trade advantage that any country is prepared to offer us, but I am not willing that the industrial establishments of this country, which have been encouraged and built up with great labour and at great sacrifice, should be destroyed in trying to get free access into the British markets. I am hostile, as a Canadian, to an arrangement of that kind.
I believe that tlie future has iu store for us a better fortune than to be limited in our trade, even with Great Britain and the islands beyond the sea. I believe that the development that is taking place in this country of ours gives promise of a condition of affairs that will enable Canada to take a more important place in tlie trade, not of the empire only, but of the entire world. It is only recently that we are beginning to realize tlie tremendous potentialities of tills Canada of oui-s, tlie magnificent natural re-
sources that are the heritage of the Canadian people from the Atlantic to the Pacific. It is only now that capitalists are beginning to discover the magnificent mineral wealth stored up in the womb of nature, and they tell us that they are in a position in reference to steel, the great trade regulator, apparently, the great trade barometer of the world, where we can manufacture it $5 or $0 a ton cheaper than it can be made at Pittsburg. Within a short period of time we will be among the principal iron and steel producers in the world. Should we not halt before we tie ourselves up to a little bit of an arrangement that will stimulate our trade slightly with the islands beyoml the sea, and will lose to us the tremendous possibilities that appear to be so near us in the future ?1 I say yes. I say let Canada have her liberty. Let us keep the right to make what trade arrangements we like with Great Britain. Let us, if we choose, give to Great Britain a preference, and let us *take it away if we find it to our interest. Let us make trade arrangement's with Germany, if necessary, that will advance the interests of our own people; let us make trade arrangements with the .United States, if necessary, that will add to the comforts and happiness of our people; but do not let us tie our hands with entangling alliances, even with Great Britain and those other Britons beyond the sea. I am a Canadian first, I want this Canada of ours to prosper. I do not want to be crippled in our liberty to do the best we can by nationality or by any other tie.
Now, Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to say a few words more upon this question, but having quoted the testimony of those distinguished men that you have heard, that there is no possibility of getting a preference except upon the basis of free trade, it would be a waste of time to give my own opinion; and X would not have quoted those men but for the fact that they occupy positions so eminent as statesmen of Great Britain. It is simply a dream on the part of our hon. friends opposite to try to get through the second part of the resolution.
But what about the third part ? Let me examine that for a few moments.
This House is further of opinion that equivalent or adequate duties should be imposed by Canada upon the products and manufactures of countries not within the empire in all cases where such countries fail to admit Canadian products and manufactures upon fair terms.
Now, that is a resolution that appears quite reasonable, that is a resolution that I most heartily endorse. But, I claim it is a resolution that is not necessary to present here to-night. That is the law of the land today. Three or four years ago that was made the law of the land. That is exactly what we have been doing. But our friends opposite have been sleeping during the past four years, and now they trot out a resolution that they want us to endorse, and 55i
say that we should have two tariff ptolicies, one for the people who use us well, and one for the people who do not. Why, that is the policy of the present government, that is what gave rise to the preference. We realized that Great Britain was the only country in the world that had been treating us as we thought right by admitting our goods free within her borders) and we selected her out from the world to enjoy a special benefit under our double-headed trade policy, a benefit that now amounts to 33J per cent. Our hon. friends opposite remind us of ltip Van Winkle who slept for so long a time. They have been sleeping for four years, and now they try to make us believe that they have discovered a remedy for some of the ills that we are supposed to suffer from. No, this principle has been in force, it is the law of the land now; its wider applicability will doubtless engage the attention of the government. I am satisfied to leave our case in the hands of the government who, for the past four years, have managed our affairs with signal ability, with great fidelity and in the Interest of the people. X have not the slightest doubt that the negotiations that are going on between our government and Germany will result in more good than the speech that was made by the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) to-night on that same question. I am prepared to assist the government, I am prepared to leave the destinies of the country in their hands, and my reason for it is that during the past four years this country has been so exceptionally well governed that we can look forward with confidence to a continuation of that kind of government, and a continuation of that prosperity which this country has enjoyed from the time the present government took control of affairs until the present moment.

I have heard Liberal members of this House tell tiie farmers that the duty has been reduced from 35 per cent to 30 per cent or 25 per cent on what kind of articles ? Shovels, spades, pronged forks, and other small articles in which the farmers invest only a few cents every year ; but of these large items, in which they invest a great deal of money, there has not been a single dollar's worth brought in under the preferential tariff, but they are subjected to duties ranging from 25 per cent to 35 per cent.
Now, passing from the trade question. I desire to discuss another feature of the government's policy. The government, and especially the Minister of the Interior, have taken great credit for what they are pleased to term the inauguration of a vigorous immigration policy. But wherein does their policy differ from that of their predecessors?
Wliat new feature has been introduced of a meritorious character that would warrant them in claiming special credit for their efforts in this direction ? If spending about twice the amount of money as their, predecessors did for immigration purposes ; if by largely increasing the number of agents and affording comfortable berths for numerous political friends ; if in order to pad out the immigration returns to make as good a showing numerically as possible for this large outlay, it is desirable to have the country flooded with thousands of Southern European immigrants who are totally unfitted for pioneer life in a new country, and who have in many instances become a burden on the public treasury ; if the system in vogue lor calculating the number of immigrants who become permanent settlers in our country is the one formerly condemned by those now in power, as one entirely misleading and unreliable; while no reliable method has been adopted to ascertain accurately the number of settlers who have actually remained in Canada ; if, I say, these are tlie features on which the government and its friends base their reasons for claiming that they are entitled to the approbation of the electorate, for this so-called .vigorous immigration policy, then X am quite willing they should be judged on those grounds, and am not in doubt as to the verdict.

I wish to call the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that he is going somewhat outside of the question, and I may be permitted to state now what the rule is. When the motion to go into Committee of Ways and Means is before the House, any question may be discussed ; but when some amendment has been moved, only the subject mentioned in the amendment can be discussed. If we turn to Bour-inot, at page 549, we see the rule well stated :
When an amendment has been moved to the question for the Speaker to leave the Chair, discussion should be propqrly confined to its subject-matter.
This rule has always been observed in England and has always been observed here also. I do not find anything in the amendment under which the question of immigration could be brought up.

Would you mind reading the.amendment, Mr. Speaker ?
Mr. SPEAKER read the amendment.
I think my remarks are quite germane to that motion, which deals with the question of protection to our labouring classes.

The immigration policy of the government and the question of protection are two different questions altogether. The rule has been observed so far, and I think it would be well not to bring into discussion any other questions than the
questions which are dealt with in the amendment.

Surely-if you will allow me, without taking exception to your ruling-it is possible to refer to the condition of the labouring classes under the question of the protection of the labouring classes, which is mentioned in the amendment. Is it not possible for my hon. friend, under that part of the amendment, to refer to the classes in the North-west whose condition has been rendered so difficult by the importation of all these aliens into the country ? There is,
I	think, very great latitude given to those who address the House on an amendment to the motion to go into Supply or into Committee of Ways and Means. In fact, it has been the custom in the past, certainly since I have been in parliament, to allow the very greatest latitude on such occasions. We have perhaps drifted away from the rules in that respect, but we have discussed almost every grievance imaginable under such motions, and unless we depart from that custom, whether it; is the rule or not,
I think we should allow some latitude.

I would not like to make any rule contrary to what has been the practice in previous years. In fact. I have looked over the authorities on the question, and it is very clear to me that when an amendment is moved to the motion that the House go into Committee of Supply, the question which should be discussed then is only the question which is mentioned in the amendment. Besides, I think the hon. member is quite mistaken when he says that it has been the custom in late years to discuss general questions under an amendment. The question was discussed in 1878 and in 1885, and it was decided in those instances in our Canadian parliament that when an amendment is moved, the discussion should be confined to the subject-matter of the amendment.
Of course, my hon. friend could wait until you put the main motion, and then repeat all the remarks lie is making at present.
Certainly.
It is for that reason, perhaps, that so much latitude has been allowed in the past, because my hon. friend would merely have to suspend his remarks until the main motion was before the House.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure there will be no question as to the accuracy of the ruling you have rather suggested than given. It may be that having called the attention of the House to the rule, you will not press it too closely, because the amendment is a somewhat broad one. While I know that the rule has been departed from, so far as I have any suggestion to offer, it would be that it
