should not bo pressed too closely now, but that you should be content rather to state it as a reminder to the House. There can be no question, however, that the rule which you have laid down is a good rule, and that the more closely we keep to it the better it will be for the order of the House.

After the budget speech has been disposed of, and amendments are made to motions to go into Committee of Supply, my recollection is that we have been kept closely to the rule ; but until the budget speech has been disposed of, we have been allowed to discuss different questions. But when the budget speech is disposed of and a specific amendment made, then hou. gentlemen must coniine themselves to the amendment.
That is the case now.

You have not made a ruling, Mr. Speaker, but merely suggestions. It seems to me that my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Roche) is fairly within the rules in discussing that special part of the resolution which relates to the labouring classes. He is pointing out that these classes are not being protected as it is suggested by the resolution they should be. And as an instance of the "want of protection, he is pointing out that a very undesirable class of people are being brought into this country to displace our own labouring men.

I merely wish to point this out to hon. gentlemen. Since the amendment has been moved, I have noticed that, in some instances, there has been discussion on matters which certainly do not come within its scope. I know that every member of this House is anxious to observe the rules as much as possible, and I thought it well to state the rule so that every one should do his best to follow it as closely as possible.

I shall certainly try to keep within the rule, Mr. Speaker, and will make my remarks as brief as possible. In fact I would have concluded them by this had I not been interrupted. I was merely going on to point out that a large number of foreigners have been brought into this country to enter into unfair competition with our labouring classes and that many of our trade societies have been passing resolutions asking the government to cease this policy.
I wish to draw attention to the number of immigrants brought in during this past year and the unfair competition to which the people of Manitoba have thus been submitted. I find, according to the immigration returns, that during the past year 41,499 immigrants were brought into Canada. Of this number there were 15,916 Galicians. Doukhobors, and miscellaneous nationali-Mr. FIELDING.
ties, leaving but 25,583 of the better class of immigrants. These have cost Canada nearly half a million of money, or $434,562.61.
Mr. MeCREARY. What are you quoting from ?

I am quoting from the report for the year ending June 30th, 1900.
Mr. MeCREARY. There were no Doukhobors brought in then.

The report also claims that 14,215 settlers came in from the United States, but when we turn to the list of homestead entries, we find that there were only 1,307 entries made by people from that country and allowing 3J persons to the family, which has been the custom in the past, that only accounts for 4,182 settlers, leaving upwards of 10,000 unaccounted for. And according to the evidence given before the Agricultural Committee by the superintendent of immigration, there has been no method adopted by which the department is aware whether those people remained in this country or not. As soon as they cross the boundary line the bonus of three dollars for every male over eighteen, two dollars for every female over eighteen, and one dollar for all under that age, has been earned and the check which the conductors keep of those people is the only evidence that they are supposed to become permanent residents. These people might stay in this country but a month or two, and then go back to the United States and we would be none the wiser.
To maintain the large staff of officials we have in the immigration service in the United States, Canada paid $86,171.18 during the last fiscal year. That is what those settlers from the United States cost us. We have over 400 agents on commission or salary, and when we take into consideration the large number of Doukhobors and Galicians, and miscellaneous nationalities amounting to 15,916, the greater portion of whom, notwithstanding what hon. gentlemen opposite may say to the contrary are totally unfit for pioneer life in a new country-
Did you ever see a Doukhobor ?

Yes, the hon. gentleman does not resemble them at all. In my own constituency where several thousand of those Galicians are located in colonies, where they were dumped down so that they may retain their old habits, and refuse to become assimilated with the general public, there was, during the late campaign, no feature of the government policy which came in for so much denunciation at the hands of the electors, both Liberals and Conservatives as this feature of their immigration policy.
Doukliobors or Galicians ?

Both. Our provincial government finds it necessary, because of this large influx of ignorant and uneducated people, to bring in a compulsory educational Bill at this session of the legislature and it is not right that they should be compelled to incur a largely increased expenditure for this purpose, that they can ill afford, on account of the policy of the Minister of the Interior. And I hope in this connection that this government 'will hand over to the province of Manitoba the school lands and the school funds now held in trust for that province and properly belonging to it, to be administered by the local authorities for educational purposes, as they are in a much better position to do so to better advantage than the Dominion government can possibly hope to be.
It has been claimed by our opponents that the days of the exodus are past, and our people no longer seek homes in the country to the south of us. But, I find on looking at the Trade and Navigation Returns that settlers effects to the amount of $1.0yj,53ii, were exported from our country during the last year, which is a pretty good index that the exodus against which they declaimed so loudly in years gone by, is still in existence.
Railway subsidies and steamship subventions which came in for so much denunciation at the hands of hon. gentlemen opposite when they were on this side of the House, I notice are still being voted as in the days of the Conservative administration only more so. Millions of dollars of public funds are annually voted for railways without any adequate return to the people, which has possibly done more to create that agitation for government ownership, an agitation that first arose in the progressive province of Manitoba, and which is gaining force every day in other portions of the Dominion, than almost any other act of the government.
In the matter of steamship subventions, our farmers were told that the country was bonusing vessels to ply between Australia and Vancouver to bring into unfair competition with our mutton the mutton from the Australian colony. They did not tell the farmers that before a pound of that mutton could be landed on Canadian territory it had to pay a duty of 35 per cent under Conservative administration. Actually Liberal campaginers hawked auout cans of Australian mutton as an illustration of the unfair competition our farmers were being subjected to. After carrying on such a warfare you would imagine these gentlemen, on coming into power, would have taken the first opportunity either to abolish the steamship subventions or at least to raise the duties, and thus give more protection to our farmers.
Did they do so ? Why, on the contrary we see that steamship subventions are continued as much as they ever were in the past ; and not only that, but, mutton is being imported in increased quantities under the tariff which gives a preference of 33J per cent. In looking up the Trade and Navigation Returns, I found that in 1S9G we imported into Canada 22,299 pounds of mutton, the duty being then 35 per cent. Last year, ending 30th June, 1900, we imported the enormous quantity of 565,401 pounds, which paid a duty reduced by 331 per cent. So, if our farmers were suffering and burdened by this keen competition in 1896, how much keener must that competition be when thirty times as much mutton is being imported under the reduction of 331 per cent. When the tariff was submitted to the House in 1897 by the present government, it created a great deal of dissatisfaction amongst the western people, and even among the western representatives, because they knew the pledges upon which they had secured their seats. They knew that promises were held out to the people that they should get their raw material free. When the tariff was brought down the Liberal speakers had to do what they could to let themselves down easy. They told us that, of course, we could not expect the government, at one feel swoop- to use a favourite expression of the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright)-to give us free trade. We were to have free trade on the instalment plan. But year after year lias gone by, and now instalments are overdue. No further instalments have been paid, and free trade- on the instalment plan has not been effected, and is not the shibboleth of the Liberal party to-day. Free agricultural implements was the cry of the past. We heard denunciations of the rebates on duties paid to the manufacturers of implements to enable them to send machines to farmers living in foreign countries thousands of miles away, to enable them to buy those implements cheaply, and to compete with our own farmers at an advantage. I find by the return brought down in response to a motion presented by myself that these drawbacks are still continued, and that, for the year ending 30th June last, they amounted to 8245,151.46. Now, I might go on and comment upon the extravagance of the government, but that point has been so fully covered that I need not occupy the time of the House. We all know that the public debt, which, we were promised would be reduced, has been increased by $7,000,000 : that the expenditures which were to have been reduced by one, two, or three millions, have gone up by fourteen millions; that the taxation of the country, which was to have been cut down has also been increased by

several millions-and still tlie carnival of extravagance goes merrily on. It is time tliat this government should call a halt to the useless waste of public money. If they are not able, during a time of great prosperity, when we have great expansion in our imports and our exports, when the trade of the country has been leaping up as it has been-if they are not able, notwithstanding that millions of dollars have been wrung out of the pockets of the people as a surplus by unnecessary and unjust taxation, to reduce our expenditure or to apply any portion of the surplus to reduce the national debt, how can we expect to effect such a reduction when we are sliding down the wave, upon the crest of which we now are, according to the Finance Minister. In the time of prosperity wise statesmen prepare for adversity. Otherwise the reaction that is sure to set in will create a commercial panic, and already there seems some sign of an approaching period of depression. While we are not pessimists-and, in that respect we differ from hou. gentlemen on the other side, for we do not believe in decrying the fair fame of our country for the sake of gaining a petty political advantage-yet, as citizens of the country, when we see the government drifting recklessly along, it is our duty to warn them of the approaching storm so that by cutting down their expenditure, and by judicious admiuistratiou, they may fortify the country against commercial disaster. In accordance with my usual custom, I will not trespass long upon the patience of the House, but will content myself with these remarks, seeing that the subject has been so thoroughly threshed out.
